items.title: Session-wide MEDIA: dedup silently swallows explicit "send it again" requests

labels.name: needs-decision
labels.description: Awaiting maintainer decision before any implementation

labels.name: sweeper:risk-message-delivery
labels.description: Sweeper risk: may drop, duplicate, misroute, or suppress messages

items.body:
**Version:** 0.19.0 (main @ 84858d7)
**Area:** gateway delivery pipeline (`gateway/platforms/base.py`)
**Platform observed:** Telegram (the guard is platform-agnostic)

## Summary

The history-dedup guard in the delivery pipeline drops any `MEDIA:<path>` whose path was already delivered earlier in the session - unconditionally, for the whole session lifetime, and without logging anything.
This makes it impossible for an agent to fulfill an explicit user request to re-send a file, and the failure mode is invisible: the directive is stripped from the reply text, so the user sees the agent say "here it is" with no attachment, and the operator finds nothing in the logs.

## Where

- `gateway/platforms/base.py`, dispatch site (~line 5455): after `extract_media()` + `filter_media_delivery_paths()`, `media_files` is filtered against `_history_media_paths_for_session(session_key)`.
- `gateway/platforms/base.py` ~line 3237: `_history_media_paths_for_session()` scans the entire persisted transcript (minus the current assistant turn).
- `gateway/run.py:1479`: `_collect_history_media_paths()`.
- The same history filter is applied to `local_files` a few lines below the `media_files` filter.

The guard's purpose is sound (a model echoing an old `MEDIA:` tag from history should not re-upload the file - the comment cites exactly that), but the implementation cannot distinguish an accidental echo from a deliberate re-send.

## Reproduction

1. Have the agent produce and deliver a file: reply containing `MEDIA:/path/to/file.png` -> file arrives.
2. In a later turn, user asks: "send me that file again."
3. Agent replies with the same `MEDIA:/path/to/file.png`.

**Expected:** file is delivered again (the user explicitly asked), or at minimum the suppression is logged.

**Actual:** the tag is stripped from the visible text, nothing is delivered, nothing is logged. Gateway log signature is the only trace - the char count shrinks between the two lines, with no `Delivering ... attachment(s)` line following:

```
INFO gateway.run: response ready: ... response=104 chars
INFO gateway.platforms.base: [Telegram] Sending response (36 chars) to ...
```

(In our case the agent had rendered a flyer and sent it once during layout iteration; when the user then asked "OK, send me this Friday's flyer" the agent correctly reused the freshly rendered file's path and the delivery was silently suppressed. The user asked "Where", the agent re-emitted the path, and it was suppressed again.)

## Why the current heuristic overreaches

- It keys on the file path for the whole session. Long-lived DM sessions (ours is 140+ messages) accumulate a permanent blocklist of every file ever sent.
- A deliberate re-send emits the path in a *fresh assistant turn* in response to a *user request* - but the guard sees only "path seen before".
- Suppression is silent both to the user-facing text (the tag is stripped, so the reply reads as if the file was attached) and to the logs (the `media_files` filter has no counterpart to the `Skipping unsafe MEDIA directive path` warning that `filter_media_delivery_paths` emits).

## Suggested fixes (any subset helps)

1. **Log the suppression** (smallest change, biggest observability win):
   `logger.info("[%s] Suppressing %d MEDIA path(s) already delivered in this session: %s", ...)`.
   This turns a multi-hour mystery into a 2-minute log grep.
2. **Narrow the window.** Dedupe against the previous assistant turn only (that is where genuine echo bugs like #29131 live), or add a short TTL / last-N-turns bound, instead of the whole transcript.
3. **Respect freshness.** Skip suppression when the file's mtime is newer than the turn in which its path was last delivered - a re-rendered artifact at the same path is new content, not an echo.
4. **Escape hatch.** Support an explicit directive (e.g. `[[resend]]`) that bypasses the history dedup for that response, so skills/agents can deliberately re-deliver. Mirrors the existing all-or-nothing semantics of `[[as_document]]` / `[[audio_as_voice]]`.

Our current workaround is a skill-level instruction to `cp` the file to a fresh unique filename before re-sending, which works but re-uploads identical bytes under a growing pile of duplicate files - exactly what the dedup was presumably trying to avoid.

items.title: gateway: long-lived Telegram sessions grow unbounded (353+ turns) with no rotation, eventually poison every subsequent request

labels.name: comp/agent
labels.description: Core agent runtime: loop, agent_init, prompt builder, context-compression, responses endpoint

labels.name: sweeper:implemented-on-main
labels.description: Sweeper: behavior already present on current main

labels.name: sweeper:risk-session-state
labels.description: Sweeper risk: may lose/corrupt/mis-associate session or context state

items.body:
## Summary

A long-running gateway session accumulates turns indefinitely with no rotation, summarization, or checkpoint. On a 24/7 Telegram deployment, a single conversation session reached **353 history turns in ~10 hours** (session started 08:08 AM, still active at 18:46 PM). Beyond a few hundred turns the message array becomes fragile: `message-alternation violations` accumulate every turn, are silently "repaired" before each request, and eventually the provider begins returning empty content arrays that trigger the retry loop in `agent/conversation_loop.py`. From the user's side this presents as `⚠️ Invalid API response after 3 retries: response time 37.7s` on *every subsequent message* until the gateway is restarted — session state is effectively poisoned with no recovery path short of process kill.

## Evidence (from a production instance)

```
2026-07-28 18:35:28  inbound message: platform=telegram msg='Are you working'
2026-07-28 18:35:28  conversation turn: session=20260728_080829_41032126 model=claude-fable-5 history=351
2026-07-28 18:35:30  Repaired 1 message-alternation violations before request (session=20260728_080829_41032126)
2026-07-28 18:35:39  Invalid API response (retry 1/3): response.content invalid (not a non-empty list) | Provider: model=claude-fable-5
2026-07-28 18:35:50  Invalid API response (retry 2/3): response.content invalid (not a non-empty list)
2026-07-28 18:36:07  Invalid API response after 3 retries.
2026-07-28 18:36:07  response ready: platform=telegram chat=… time=39.4s api_calls=1 response=60 chars
2026-07-28 18:36:07  Transient agent failure … persisting user message so conversation context is preserved on retry.
```

Same session, three consecutive user turns (history=351, 352, 353) all failed identically. `Repaired N message-alternation violations` count grew by one each turn (1 → 2 → 3), i.e. the repair pass was doing more work each round without ever addressing the root cause. `launchctl kickstart -k gui/501/ai.hermes.gateway` immediately restored service by dropping the session.

## Why this is different from #71999

#71999 covers a **guard false-fire** on the persisted-vs-live length comparison caused by alternation-repair *merging* pairs at restore time. That's a warning-noise / bypass-cleanup problem on tool-use turns. This report is different in two ways:

1. It's about **unbounded session growth itself** — no cap, no rotation, no auto-checkpoint. The same session at 353 turns will still be 500, 1000, 2000 turns tomorrow if nothing intervenes.
2. The alternation repair here is not merging split tool-call pairs benignly (as in #71999). It is generating a payload that the *provider* accepts (HTTP 200) but returns `content: []` for, which then poisons every subsequent turn until process restart. See sibling issue [FOLLOWUP — will link once filed] on the retry-loop side of that failure.

## Suggested fix

1. **Session rotation ceiling.** Introduce a configurable soft cap (e.g. `agent.max_session_turns` default 200) that, when exceeded, either (a) rolls over to a fresh session with a summarized carry-forward message, or (b) triggers the existing context-compression path proactively rather than only on token pressure. On Telegram-shaped deployments where users never `/reset`, this is the only backstop.
2. **Health signal on repair-count trend.** `Repaired N message-alternation violations` climbing monotonically across turns of the same session is a leading indicator of corruption. Emit a WARN (with session id) when N > threshold (e.g. 3) or grows across ≥3 consecutive turns, so operators can catch it before every request fails.
3. **Automatic recovery.** After N consecutive `Invalid API response after 3 retries` failures on the same session (e.g. 2), force a session rotation instead of continuing to serve the poisoned history. The current `Transient agent failure … persisting user message` path guarantees the *next* turn hits the same failure with `history += 1`.

## Environment

- Hermes Agent: 0.16.x (commit `3c73d1852e37`)
- Provider: Anthropic Messages API, `claude-fable-5`
- Platform: Telegram DM, 24/7 gateway (launchd, `ai.hermes.gateway`)
- Reproduction: leave a single Telegram DM session running for ~10 hours of active use; failure begins reliably somewhere past history≈300 with `claude-fable-5`.

## main is red: photon test failures on every PR's required slices (bisected)

`main`'s own tip CI is failing `Python tests / Run tests slice 2/8` and `7/8` (e.g. the check runs on 40a53ca03), which also fails every open PR's required checks. Two independent causes, both in the photon platform:

### 1. `fd4f75649` (salvage of #54514) regresses the U+FFFC deferred-attachment machinery — 4 tests

Bisect on `tests/plugins/platforms/photon/test_inbound.py::test_fffc_placeholder_no_dispatch`:

| commit | result |
|---|---|
| `afab7ed46` (adds `_pending_fffc` deferral + tests) | ✅ passes |
| `fd4f75649` fix(photon): ignore iMessage media placeholders | ❌ fails |
| current tip | ❌ fails |

The salvaged commit predates `afab7ed46`: it early-returns on `raw_text.strip() == "￼"` **before** the `_pending_fffc` registration that `afab7ed46` introduced, so the placeholder is swallowed instead of deferred. All four fffc tests fail (`test_fffc_placeholder_no_dispatch`, `test_fffc_then_attachment_cancels_timeout`, `test_fffc_timeout_fires_when_no_attachment`, `test_disconnect_cancels_pending_fffc_tasks`), and behaviorally the voice-note flow (placeholder → media follows) loses its timeout/cancel contract. Looks like a salvage-ordering conflict between #54514 and the newer deferral design — the early return probably needs to be dropped in favor of the existing `_pending_fffc` path (which already ignores the placeholder for dispatch purposes).

### 2. `e79d316a0` runtime-record tests require sidecar npm deps — 2 tests

`test_runtime_record.py::test_record_written_after_healthz_success` / `test_record_removed_on_failed_startup` call the real `_start_sidecar()`, which now raises when `sidecar_deps_installed()` is false:

```
RuntimeError: Photon sidecar deps not installed. Run: cd .../sidecar && npm install
```

Reproduces on any runner without the sidecar's `node_modules` (CI slices included). The tests need a `sidecar_deps_installed` monkeypatch (the neighboring sidecar tests already mock this seam).

Also seen red on the same slices: `tests/conformance/test_vector_generator.py::test_committed_vectors_match_regeneration` — that one passes locally for me, so it may be a separate CI-env drift.

Happy to send a PR for either fix if useful.

items.title: Desktop: mid-turn messages render above assistant output that predates them

labels.name: sweeper:risk-session-state
labels.description: Sweeper risk: may lose/corrupt/mis-associate session or context state

items.body:
### Summary

In the desktop app, a message typed **while a turn is still streaming** renders *above* assistant output that was already on screen when it was typed. From the user's side it looks like the message "jumps up" past content they just watched arrive.

### Where it comes from

`appendLiveSessionProjection` in `apps/desktop/src/app/session/hooks/use-session-actions/utils.ts` builds the projected turn in this order:

1. `inflight.user` (the prompt that started the turn)
2. `inflight.corrections` (anything typed mid-turn)
3. the `assistant-stream-${sessionId}` bubble
4. `queuedUser`

The existing comment states the intent explicitly:

> Corrections typed while the turn ran. Each is its own bubble, placed after the original prompt and **before the reply they redirected** — the same order the live transcript showed.

That's coherent as a *semantic* ordering (the correction influenced the reply, so it precedes it). The problem is that the entire in-flight turn is collapsed into a **single** assistant bubble, so "before the reply" means "before *everything* the assistant has streamed so far," including several screens of output the user had already read before typing.

It also disagrees with the live path: `mutateStream` (`use-message-stream/index.ts`) updates the streaming bubble **in place**, and `seedOptimistic` (`use-prompt-actions/submit.ts`) appends the new user message at the end — so live rendering is arrival-ordered, and only the projection on resume/reload reorders. The visible symptom is therefore a *jump*: the message appears below, then moves above on the next projection.

### Reproduce

1. Send a prompt that produces a long streaming reply (e.g. one that emits a couple of large code blocks).
2. While it is still streaming and the blocks are visible, send a short follow-up ("urgently").
3. The follow-up bubble renders above both code blocks, which predate it.

### Suggested fix

Order the projection by arrival: prompt → in-flight reply → corrections → queued. That is a two-block swap in `appendLiveSessionProjection`, and it makes the projection agree with what the live transcript already does.

If preserving the "correction precedes the reply it redirected" semantic is preferred, the alternative is to split the in-flight assistant bubble at each correction boundary, so a correction lands before only the output it actually influenced rather than before the whole turn. That is a larger change but keeps both the semantics and the visual timeline honest.

Happy to open a PR for the ordering swap if that's the direction you'd take.

### Environment

- Desktop app, macOS (Apple Silicon), remote-gateway connection mode (app on one machine, gateway on another)
- Observed on a build from `main`, late July 2026

items.title: [Feature]: add antigravity-cli as a subprocess-based provider (agy stream-json backend)

labels.name: sweeper:not-planned
labels.description: Sweeper: closed per standing maintainer policy (design direction)

items.body:
### Problem or Use Case

Users who have an active Antigravity subscription (via Google AI Pro / Antigravity) cannot use those models from within Hermes. OAuth-based integration (PR #50454) was merged but immediately reverted (#50492) due to Google policy: accounts using Gemini CLI / Antigravity / Code Assist OAuth for third-party access risk full Google account bans (Gmail/Drive included), with permanent ban on second violation. This was documented in issue #60699.
The policy risk is upstream and not going away. But since the release of agy 1.1.8, there is now a **subprocess-based alternative that avoids the OAuth issue entirely**.

Additional Context:

- Prior art: `copilot-acp` provider (`acp_adapter/`) — subprocess-based provider using CLI tool as backend
- Antigravity CLI headless docs: https://antigravity.google/docs/cli/headless#streaming-json
- Earlier OAuth attempt and revert: #50454 → #50492
- Related issue: #60699 (docs clarification for Gemini AI Pro subscription incompatibility)


### Proposed Solution

Add `antigravity-cli` as a subprocess-backed provider, following the same architectural pattern as the existing `copilot-acp` provider. Instead of making API calls or using OAuth, Hermes would shell out to the local `agy` binary in headless mode and parse its structured NDJSON output.

1. User has `agy` installed and authenticated locally (their own Antigravity subscription)
2. Hermes detects `agy` on `PATH` and offers `antigravity` as a setup option
3. At inference time, Hermes spawns:
```
   agy -p "<prompt>" --output-format stream-json --dangerously-skip-permissions --model "<model>"
```
4. Hermes parses the NDJSON event stream:
  - `init` → extract conversation_id, available tools
  - `step_update` (state: ACTIVE, step_type: agent_response) → stream `text_delta` tokens
  - `step_update` (state: DONE, step_type: tool) → capture tool_info if relevant
  - `result` → capture final response + usage stats
5. Token accounting (`input_tokens`, `output_tokens`, `thinking_tokens`, `cache_read_tokens`) is reported back to the Hermes usage tracking.
### Implementation sketch
1. **Provider detection** — Check `shutil.which("agy")` in `setup` flow
2. **ACP-style adapter** — New subprocess manager (or extend `acp_adapter`) that:
  - Spawns `agy -p` with `stream-json` output
  - Reads stdout line-by-line, parses NDJSON events
  - Yields `text_delta` chunks for streaming
  - Captures final `result` payload and maps to Hermes `Usage` model
3. **Model catalog** — Add known antigravity model slugs as discoverable models (`gemini-3.6-flash`, `gemini-3.6-pro`, etc.)
4. **`hermes setup` integration** — Add `antigravity` to the provider picker when `agy` is detected
### Open questions / risks
- **Tool call forwarding** — agy makes its own tool calls (`run_command`, `write_to_file`) in headless mode. With
`--dangerously-skip-permissions`, it auto-executes. Should Hermes suppress agy's tool layer entirely and only consume text output? Or should certain tool calls be forwarded back to Hermes?
- **Subprocess overhead** — Spawning `agy` per-turn adds ~1-2s cold-start. The `--continue` flag could maintain
conversation context across turns.
- **Conversation continuity** — agy maintains its own conversation history server-side. Should Hermes treat each turn as
a new headless invocation (`-p`), or track `conversation_id` for multi-turn?
- **Dependency weight** — `agy` binary is ~200MB+. Should be documented as an optional/external dependency, like
`docker` or `node`.

### Alternatives Considered

Antigravity SDK integration — The[`google-antigravity/antigravity`](https://github.com/google-antigravity/antigravity) SDK is another viable path. Instead of shelling out to the `agy` binary, Hermes could depend on the Python SDK directly (`pip install antigravity`) and call its programmatic API. This avoids subprocess spawn overhead, enables native streaming via SDK callbacks, and gives proper error typing and structured response handling. The tradeoff is an additional pip dependency vs. zero-install CLI wrapping. Either path avoids the Google OAuth policy risk since the SDK uses the same local credential cache as `agy`.


### Feature Type

Configuration option

### Scope

Medium (few files, < 300 lines)

### Contribution

- [ ] I'd like to implement this myself and submit a PR

### Debug Report (optional)

```shell

```

items.title: Windows: Desktop self-update can never succeed â€” applyUpdates' own SIGTERM triggers a renderer reconnect that respawns the backend before scanVenvBlockers runs

labels.name: P1
labels.description: High — major feature broken, no workaround

labels.name: sweeper:risk-compatibility
labels.description: Sweeper risk: may break existing users, config, migrations, defaults, or upgrades

labels.name: sweeper:risk-platform-windows
labels.description: Sweeper risk: may break or behave differently on native Windows

items.body:
﻿## Summary

On Windows, "Update now" in Hermes Desktop aborts every time with:

```
Update aborted: another Hermes process is using this installation.

These processes must be stopped before updating:

  PID <redacted>  python.exe  ...hermes_cli.main gateway run...
```

There are **two independent venv holders**, and the first one is created by the update flow itself. Fixing only the second still leaves the update permanently blocked, and vice versa.

Existing issues cover neighbouring symptoms but not holder (a): #62311 (external gateway/dashboard holds the shim, aborts in `releaseBackendLock`'s 15s poll), #61514 (CLI path: gateway pause orphans venv-resident children), #61898 (a *different* `updateInFlight` race â€” double-trigger during the 2.5s dwell), #43268 (closed; `uv pip install` lock contention). Ours aborts at a different site â€” the `scanVenvBlockers` preflight in `applyUpdates`, *after* the shim lock was successfully released.

## Environment

- Hermes 0.19.0, upstream commit `0f64557c06f3e878fd9ec5170b9bca7f20e2778e`
- Windows 11, Python 3.11
- Managed desktop install, venv at `<HERMES_HOME>/hermes-agent/venv`
- Reproduces 100% of the time

---

## Holder (a) â€” the self-race: the app respawns the process it is about to complain about

### Sequence (from `desktop.log`, identical on every attempt)

1. `applyUpdates` (`apps/desktop/electron/main.ts:2781`) sets `updateInFlight = true` at `main.ts:2786`.
2. `releaseBackendLockForUpdate` â†’ `releaseBackendLock` (`main.ts:2689`) SIGTERMs the primary backend, stops pool backends, force-kills the tree, polls the shim, and logs `venv shim unlocked; safe to proceed` (`main.ts:2728`). **This step genuinely succeeds.**
3. That SIGTERM drops the renderer's websocket. The renderer reconnects ~1s later â†’ `getConnection` â†’ `startHermes` â†’ `runPrimaryBackendStartup`.
4. `primary-backend-startup.ts:46` awaits `waitForLocalStart()`, which is `waitForUpdateToFinish` (registered at `main.ts:8294`).
5. **`waitForUpdateToFinish` (`main.ts:1736`) keys off the on-disk marker only** â€” `readLiveUpdateMarker(HERMES_HOME)`; if there is no marker it returns `false` immediately (`main.ts:1737-1741`). The in-process `updateInFlight` flag (`main.ts:2535`), which *is* already true, is never consulted by this gate.
6. The marker is not written until `writeUpdateMarker(HERMES_HOME, child.pid)` at `main.ts:2936` â€” i.e. **after** the scan. So during the entire window the gate is open, and the reconnect spawns a brand-new backend from the venv.
7. `scanVenvBlockers(updateRoot)` at `main.ts:2892` then finds that brand-new process and aborts with `kind === 'blocked'` (`main.ts:2894-2901`).

The ordering is the whole bug: the only guard against "start a backend while an update is running" is armed *after* the check it exists to protect.

### Proof it is self-inflicted

- The reported PID is **different on every attempt**.
- **No such process exists between attempts** â€” the app is idle, nothing holds the venv, yet the very next attempt reports a fresh PID.
- In the log, `[boot] Starting Hermes backend via ...` appears between `Hermes backend exited (SIGTERM)` and the `[updates] venv-blocked:` line. The blocker is spawned inside the update's own critical section.

### Suggested direction (proposing, not prescribing)

Make the boot gate consult the in-process flag as well as the marker â€” e.g. park when `marker || updateInFlight`, returning early only when neither is set â€” so a waiter that arrives during the pre-hand-off window blocks until either the flag clears (abort path) or the marker appears (success path). The success path already writes the marker *before* `applyUpdates` returns and clears the flag in its `finally` (`main.ts:2953`), so there is no gap where both are false. Worth checking alongside:

- **Pool backends are ungated.** `spawnPoolBackend` (around `main.ts:8000-8030`) awaits `resolveRemoteBackend`/`ensureRuntime` and spawns with no `waitForLocalStart` call anywhere in its path. `releaseBackendLock`'s `stopAllPoolBackends` kills them, so a second profile window can reconnect and respawn during the same window â€” same abort, but the PID's cmdline reads `--profile <name> serve`. A non-UI variant of the waiter would be needed there, since the existing one drives primary-window boot-progress.
- The abort branches call `startHermes().catch(() => {})` right after emitting the error, which is correct, but with a flag-aware gate that call would park for one poll tick before spawning â€” a small, acceptable latency change worth noting.

---

## Holder (b) â€” the gateway autostart Hermes installs itself

Even with (a) resolved, the update still aborts. A long-running `hermes_cli.main gateway run` process runs from the same venv interpreter and is never stopped by the desktop update flow â€” `releaseBackendLock` only tree-kills the desktop's *own* backend PIDs (primary + pool). The error message names that PID.

This is not an exotic configuration. Hermes sets up the gateway to start at logon itself: `hermes_cli/gateway_windows.py` registers a Scheduled Task (with a Startup-folder fallback via `wscript.exe`, `gateway_windows.py:456-527`), and `wscript.exe` is GUI-subsystem with no console by design. So any Windows user who has enabled the gateway ends up with a permanent venv holder that the desktop updater cannot see past and that has no window to close.

This overlaps with #62311, which proposes scanning for and tree-killing external venv holders in `releaseBackendLock`. Two additions:

- The failure surfaces at a **second, later** abort site too. Here `releaseBackendLock` reported the shim as unlocked and the abort came from the `scanVenvBlockers` preflight, so a fix that only addresses the 15s shim poll would not cover it.
- Whatever mechanism stops the gateway should account for #61514: a graceful gateway stop on Windows orphans its venv-resident children, which then trip the same guard.

---

## The error text is not actionable

`formatBlockerMessage` (`apps/desktop/electron/venv-blocker-scan.ts:178-199`) tells the user:

> Close the terminal, app, or service owning that process. If it is a remote backend, stopping it will disconnect remote clients.

Both holders are owned by Hermes itself and are invisible to the user: holder (a) is a backend the app respawned milliseconds earlier, and the gateway autostart runs without a console window, tray entry, or any UI affordance to close. There is nothing for the user to act on.

Suggestion: when a blocker's cmdline is recognisably a Hermes-owned process (backend, gateway, dashboard), say so and offer to stop it, rather than asking the user to find a window that does not exist.

## Reproduction (minimal)

1. Windows 11, managed desktop install, gateway autostart enabled.
2. Launch Hermes Desktop, let the backend connect.
3. Trigger "Update now" from the desktop UI.
4. Observed: `Update aborted: another Hermes process is using this installation.` â€” reported PID differs on every attempt; between attempts no Hermes process is running at all.

**Actual:** every desktop update attempt aborts at the venv-blocker preflight.
**Expected:** the desktop update either stops the processes it owns, or does not count them as blockers.

## Current workaround

Fully quit Hermes Desktop, stop the gateway, then run `hermes update` from the CLI with **no** force flags. This works. Note that `--force-venv` is *not* a viable escape hatch here â€” its own help text says it will "likely fail partway and strand the install half-updated" and to use it "only if you know the detected holders are false positives", and in this scenario the holders are real, live processes.

## Relevant code

- `apps/desktop/electron/main.ts:1736` â€” `waitForUpdateToFinish`, marker-only gate
- `apps/desktop/electron/main.ts:2535` â€” `let updateInFlight = false`
- `apps/desktop/electron/main.ts:2781`, `:2786` â€” `applyUpdates`, flag set
- `apps/desktop/electron/main.ts:2689`, `:2728` â€” `releaseBackendLock`, shim-unlock log
- `apps/desktop/electron/main.ts:2892-2901` â€” `scanVenvBlockers` preflight and the `venv-blocked` abort
- `apps/desktop/electron/main.ts:2936` â€” `writeUpdateMarker` (after the scan)
- `apps/desktop/electron/main.ts:2953` â€” `finally { updateInFlight = false }`
- `apps/desktop/electron/main.ts:8294` â€” `waitForLocalStart: waitForUpdateToFinish`
- `apps/desktop/electron/primary-backend-startup.ts:46` â€” `await waitForLocalStart()`
- `apps/desktop/electron/venv-blocker-scan.ts:178-199` â€” `formatBlockerMessage`

Happy to test a patch and report back with logs.

items.title: [Bug]: Token/cost accounting dies permanently on installs already at schema_version >= 22 â€” the session_model_usage PK rebuild is unreachable behind `current_version < 22`

labels.name: comp/agent
labels.description: Core agent runtime: loop, agent_init, prompt builder, context-compression, responses endpoint

labels.name: P1
labels.description: High — major feature broken, no workaround

labels.name: sweeper:risk-session-state
labels.description: Sweeper risk: may lose/corrupt/mis-associate session or context state

labels.name: area/usage-cost
labels.description: Token accounting, usage reporting, billing, cost tracking

items.body:
﻿## Summary

On installs whose `state.db` had already reached `schema_version >= 22` before the `task`
dimension was added to `session_model_usage`, **every** token and cost write fails, permanently
and silently. The per-model upsert in `_record_model_usage()` names a 6-column conflict target
while the live table still carries the old 5-column PRIMARY KEY, so SQLite raises:

```
WARNING hermes_state: async token accounting: apply failed (session=<redacted>):
ON CONFLICT clause does not match any PRIMARY KEY or UNIQUE constraint
```

The migration block that would rebuild the table with the correct PK is gated behind
`if current_version < 22:`, and the version bump to `SCHEMA_VERSION` happens *after* that chain â€”
so on a DB already at 22/23 the repair is unreachable on every subsequent open. It never
self-heals.

Observed on a real install: from the day the DB reached version 23 onward, **100% of sessions
recorded zero tokens** â€” cost/insights reporting reads $0 / 0 tokens indefinitely.

**Environment:** Hermes 0.19.0, upstream commit `0f64557c06f3e878fd9ec5170b9bca7f20e2778e`, Windows 11, Python 3.11.

## Root cause

1. `SCHEMA_VERSION = 23` â€” `hermes_state.py:286`.
2. `SCHEMA_SQL` declares `PRIMARY KEY (session_id, model, billing_provider, billing_base_url,
   billing_mode, task)` â€” `hermes_state.py:1319-1338`. This is only applied to **new** databases.
3. The upsert names the same 6 columns â€”
   `hermes_state.py:5802`: `ON CONFLICT(session_id, model, billing_provider, billing_base_url, billing_mode, task)`.
4. The only code that converts an existing 5-column-PK table to the 6-column shape is the
   rename â†’ CREATE â†’ `INSERTâ€¦SELECT` â†’ DROP â†’ recreate-index block at
   `hermes_state.py:3782-3844`, entered only under `if current_version < 22:`
   (`hermes_state.py:3782`).
5. The version bump to `SCHEMA_VERSION` happens after that chain
   (`hermes_state.py:3903-3917`). Once the recorded version is â‰¥ 22, step 4 can never run again.
6. `_reconcile_columns()` (`hermes_state.py:3455-3467`, docstring: *"Version-gated migration
   blocks are no longer needed for ADD COLUMN"*) then re-adds a **bare nullable** `task` column
   via `ALTER TABLE`. That is what makes this so easy to miss: the column *is* present, so nothing
   looks wrong, but it is not part of the PK.

Resulting live schema on an affected install:

```sql
CREATE TABLE session_model_usage (
  ...
  last_seen REAL,
  "task" TEXT DEFAULT ''                      -- ALTER-TABLE shape, not in the key
  PRIMARY KEY (session_id, model, billing_provider, billing_base_url, billing_mode)
);
```

No `session_model_usage_v21` leftover exists, confirming the rebuild is not half-done â€” it simply
never runs.

## Why this is worse than a per-model-row problem

`_record_model_usage()` runs **inside the caller's write transaction, after the `sessions`
UPDATE** â€” its own docstring says so (`hermes_state.py:5758-5760`):

> Runs inside the caller's write transaction (after the ``sessions`` UPDATE) so the per-model rows
> stay consistent with the summary row.

So the failed upsert aborts the whole transaction and the **per-session summary columns are lost
too**: `sessions.input_tokens`, `output_tokens`, `estimated_cost_usd`, `actual_cost_usd` all stay
0/NULL. It is caught and logged as a WARNING and never raised, so the user sees zero cost data
with no error anywhere in the UI or CLI.

Net effect on an affected install: the last successful `session_model_usage` write is the day
before the DB crossed to version 23; every session created after that has zero tokens, forever.
The `task`-attribution feature has never recorded a single non-empty row there.

## Am I affected? (one-line check)

```sql
-- 0 means affected: the `task` column exists but is not part of the PK
SELECT COUNT(*) FROM pragma_table_info('session_model_usage') WHERE name='task' AND pk > 0;
```

Or just look for `ON CONFLICT clause does not match any PRIMARY KEY or UNIQUE constraint` in
`errors.log`.

## Minimal repro

Against a stock 0.19.0 install, on a throwaway `state.db`:

1. Recreate `session_model_usage` with the **old** 5-column PK
   (`session_id, model, billing_provider, billing_base_url, billing_mode`), then
   `ALTER TABLE session_model_usage ADD COLUMN task TEXT DEFAULT ''`.
2. `UPDATE schema_version SET version = 23;`
3. Start Hermes and run any session that produces a model call.

**Actual:** the migration chain skips the rebuild (`current_version` is already 23),
`_reconcile_columns` leaves the bare `task` column in place, and every accounting write fails with
the ON CONFLICT warning. `sessions.input_tokens` stays 0 and `session_model_usage` gets no new
rows. Restarting, updating, or reinstalling does not fix it.

**Expected:** the schema is repaired to the 6-column PK regardless of the recorded version, and
token/cost accounting works.

The organic path to this state is presumably: a DB that reached version 22 (or 23) under a build
whose `SCHEMA_SQL` still had the 5-column PK, then upgraded to a build that added `task` to the
key.

## Suggested fix direction (proposing, not prescribing)

The codebase already has exactly the right pattern for this in the same file:
`_heal_gateway_routing_pk()` (`hermes_state.py:3499`, called unconditionally from
`hermes_state.py:3599`), which is an idempotent, shape-detecting healer. Replacing the
`current_version < 22` gate at `hermes_state.py:3782` with a sibling healer modeled on it â€”
reusing the existing rename/create/copy/drop/reindex body already written at
`hermes_state.py:3795-3844` â€” would make the repair reachable on affected installs, and would be a
no-op on healthy ones.

Two details that seem worth handling if you go that route:

- The copy step probably wants `INSERT OR IGNORE`. Collapsing rows into a wider key cannot collide
  when the old PK is a strict prefix of the new one and all `task` values are `''`, but a generic
  healer that hits a collision would raise `sqlite3.IntegrityError`, which is **not** caught by the
  surrounding `except sqlite3.OperationalError` and would surface as a startup crash.
- `session_model_usage` has an FK to `sessions` with `ON DELETE CASCADE`; the rebuild should run in
  one transaction with foreign-key handling explicit so the constraint survives.

Independently of the migration bug, it may be worth reconsidering whether a failure in
`_record_model_usage()` should be allowed to take the enclosing transaction â€” and therefore the
`sessions` summary row â€” down with it. Degrading to "per-model attribution missing" would be much
less damaging than "no accounting at all", and would have made this far more visible.

Note that historical token data for the affected window is unrecoverable either way; a fix only
restores future accounting.

## Relationship to existing issues

I looked for an existing report and did not find this specific defect:

- **#67764** (`cost_status` overwritten across SQL / in-memory / `/insights`) â€” same area
  (`area/billing`, `area/usage-cost`) and it touches the same `session_model_usage` UPSERT, but it
  is a **different defect**: it is about which status value wins among successful writes. Here the
  write never lands at all, so the priority ladder is moot. Worth noting for whoever lands #67790:
  on an affected install none of that SQL executes, so a fix there is untestable until this is
  resolved.
- **#71578** (token counters record 0 when `billing_provider` is NULL) â€” same *symptom* (zero
  tokens), different discriminator. There the split is per-session on `billing_provider`; here
  **every** session on the install is zero, and the DB raises an explicit ON CONFLICT error.
- **#71480** / **#69603** â€” also in the `state.db` schema-surgery area, but they concern
  `sqlite_master` corruption and concurrent DDL, not an unreachable version-gated migration.

items.title: Feature Request: Tool Allowlist with block-level enforcement

labels.name: comp/cli
labels.description: CLI entry point, hermes_cli/, setup wizard

labels.name: sweeper:implemented-on-main
labels.description: Sweeper: behavior already present on current main

items.body:
## Feature Request: Tool Allowlist with block-level enforcement

### Problem

Claude Code implements a powerful mechanism called \`allowed-tools\` that defines an explicit **whitelist** of tools an agent may call. Any tool not in the whitelist is physically rejected before execution.

Example from \`.claude/commands/commit-push-pr.md\`:
\`\`\`yaml
allowed-tools:
  - Bash(git checkout --branch:*)
  - Bash(git add:*)
  - Bash(git status:*)
  - Bash(git push:*)
  - Bash(git commit:*)
  - Bash(gh pr create:*)
\`\`\`

Hermes currently has no equivalent. The agent can invoke any tool regardless of context. This leads to:
- Subagents or cron jobs running dangerous bash commands
- Unintended tool usage in sensitive contexts
- No enforcement of "least privilege" per workspace/task

### Proposed Solution

Add a \`toolsets\` or \`allowed-tools\` config that supports:
1. **Tool whitelist** per workspace or per cron job
2. **PreTool block** — not just warn, but actually reject the tool call
3. **Graceful degradation** — return an error message instead of executing

Reference: Claude Code hookify plugin supports \`action: block\` on PreTool hooks.

### Use Cases

- Cron jobs that should only run read-only commands
- Subagents with limited scope
- "Safe mode" for untrusted workspace contexts
- Implementing CLAUDE.md-style rules as hard constraints

### Priority

High — this directly impacts task accuracy and safety in automated contexts.

### Labels

feature-request, security, toolsets

items.body:
## Summary

When creating a new session from within a Project (click project in sidebar → Cmd+N), the session is correctly attached to the project on the backend (`project_list` confirms `active_id` matches), but the **left sidebar groups it under "Home"** instead of under the project it was created from.

## Steps to reproduce

1. Open the desktop app
2. Click a project in the left sidebar (e.g. "0 | Tauli Tailor")
3. Press **Cmd+N** to create a new session
4. Observe: the new session appears under the **"Home"** group in the sidebar, not under "0 | Tauli Tailor"

## Expected behavior

The new session should appear grouped under the project it was created from (e.g. "0 | Tauli Tailor").

## Actual behavior

The session appears under "Home" in the sidebar, even though:
- `project_list` returns the correct `active_id` for the project
- The session workspace/cwd correctly points to the project path
- All tools and file operations run in the correct project directory

The attachment is correct at the data layer; only the **sidebar grouping/rendering** is wrong.

## Environment

- macOS 26.5.1
- Hermes Desktop app
- Session created from project context via Cmd+N

## Related

- #53004 (broader Projects paradigm issues — sidebar grouping)
- #71232 (project sidebar rendering issues)

This is a narrower, specific case: the session-to-project binding works, but the sidebar UI does not reflect it.

items.body:
## Context

Follow-up to #71226 / PR #73809.

PR #73809 removed the lifespan-time `_warm_gateway_module()` prewarm, which was the confirmed root cause of the desktop boot loop: a `run_in_executor` thread importing `hermes_cli.gateway` doesn't isolate the event loop from GIL retention during a cold import (Windows `.pyc` compilation + Defender real-time scan), so `/api/health` and the WebSocket `gateway.ready` handshake starved past the desktop client's connect timeout.

## Residual gap

Removing the prewarm doesn't eliminate the cold import — it defers it. `hermes_cli.gateway` now imports lazily on first real use, e.g. the first `/api/status` call (`_resolve_restart_drain_timeout`, still wrapped in `run_in_executor`). That first call can still briefly retain the GIL the same way the removed prewarm did.

## Why this isn't urgent

- Desktop readiness now uses `/api/health`, which never touches `hermes_cli.gateway` — the boot-loop race is closed.
- `/api/status` already carries a generous timeout budget from PR #71104 (45s total, 5s per probe rung), which absorbs an occasional slow first call.
- No reports of a stall specifically on `/api/status` after the boot-loop fix.

## Possible follow-up (not scoped/committed yet)

Move the gateway-module prewarm to a genuinely isolated **subprocess** (e.g. detached `subprocess.Popen` that just runs the import) instead of a thread. A subprocess doesn't share the GIL with the main process, so it can pre-compile `.pyc` and warm the OS file-system cache without any risk of starving the event loop — while still paying the cold-import cost proactively instead of on first real request.

Deliberately not done as part of #71226 / PR #73809: it adds process lifecycle (spawn, logs, cancellation-on-shutdown, cross-platform spawn behavior) for a risk that currently has no live symptom. Worth revisiting if `/api/status` cold-start latency becomes a reported problem.

## Scope for whoever picks this up

- Decide if a subprocess prewarm is worth the added complexity, or if the existing `/api/status` timeout budget is sufficient long-term.
- If pursued: spawn a detached subprocess at lifespan start that only imports `hermes_cli.gateway` (no shared state needed — the goal is just `.pyc` compilation + OS page cache warmth), with clean shutdown handling.
- Add a regression test analogous to the one added in PR #73809 (GIL-retention simulation via `sys.setswitchinterval`, not `time.sleep`) proving the subprocess approach doesn't starve `/api/health` even under simulated Defender-scan-speed cold imports.

items.title: [Bug]: Flaky test - test_detach_keeps_draining_into_buffer intermittently fails

labels.name: comp/cli
labels.description: CLI entry point, hermes_cli/, setup wizard

items.body:
### Bug Description

tests/test_pty_session.py::test_detach_keeps_draining_into_buffer fails intermittently with:

  `assert b'one' == b'onetwo'`
                                                                                                               
The buffer only contains b"one" — the b"two" chunk has not been consumed by the background drain task yet. This is a timing-dependent race in the test code itself, not in the production code.

### Steps to Reproduce

Run the following reproduction script 3-5 times next to test_pty_session.py:

``` python
import asyncio, sys
sys.path.insert(0, '.')
from hermes_cli.pty_session import PtySession
class FakeBridge:
    def __init__(self, chunks):
        self._chunks = list(chunks)
        self.written = bytearray()
        self.closed = False
        self.resized = None
    def read(self, timeout):
        return self._chunks.pop(0) if self._chunks else b""
    def write(self, data):
        self.written.extend(data)
    def resize(self, cols, rows):
        self.resized = (cols, rows)
    def close(self):
        self.closed = True
async def trial():
    bridge = FakeBridge([b"one", b"", b"two"])
    s = PtySession("k", bridge, buffer_cap=1024, read_timeout=0.01)
    await s.start()
    ws = object()
    s._ws = ws
    s.attached = True
    s.detach(ws)
    await asyncio.sleep(0.05)
    return s.buffer.snapshot()
async def main():
    fail = 0
    for i in range(1000):
        snap = await trial()
        if snap != b"onetwo":
            fail += 1
    print(f"{fail}/{1000} FAILED")
asyncio.run(main())
```

### Expected Behavior

assert replay == b"onetwo" should pass 100% of the time. The buffer should always contain both b"one" and b"two" after the 50ms wait.

### Actual Behavior

The assertion fails intermittently — reproduced ~880/1000 failures locally.

### Affected Component

Other

### Messaging Platform (if gateway-related)

_No response_

### Debug Report

```shell
Not applicable — this is a test flakiness issue, not a runtime bug.
```

### Operating System

Windows 10 build 15063

### Python Version

3.11.15

### Hermes Version

v0.19.0

### Additional Logs / Traceback (optional)

```shell

```

### Root Cause Analysis (optional)

The test uses await asyncio.sleep(0.05) to wait for the background drain task to consume all data. Both the drain loop and the test yield cooperatively via await asyncio.sleep(). The event loop's scheduling order is non-deterministic under load — sometimes the test resumes before the drain has consumed b"two".

### Proposed Fix (optional)

Several options (open to maintainer preference):

1. Polling loop - replace sleep(0.05) with a retry loop checking buffer.snapshot() every 10ms
2. asyncio.Event - have PtySession._drain signal when data is written
3. Mock run_in_executor to be synchronous - eliminate the yield point entirely

I'm happy to submit a PR whichever direction the maintainers prefer.

### Are you willing to submit a PR for this?

- [x] I'd like to fix this myself and submit a PR

items.title: Codex OAuth device-code cancel does not stop worker; can save credentials to wrong profile (P1)

labels.name: comp/cli
labels.description: CLI entry point, hermes_cli/, setup wizard

labels.name: sweeper:risk-security-boundary
labels.description: Sweeper risk: may affect sandboxing, auth, credentials, or sensitive data

labels.name: sweeper:risk-compatibility
labels.description: Sweeper risk: may break existing users, config, migrations, defaults, or upgrades

items.body:
## Summary

Cancelling a pending OpenAI Codex device-code OAuth login (dashboard "Cancel" button) does not stop the background worker. If the user approves the device code at OpenAI's side *after* clicking cancel, the worker still exchanges the code and saves the tokens — and can save them into the **wrong profile**.

 

## Root cause

`DELETE /api/providers/oauth/sessions/{session_id}` (`cancel_oauth_session`) only pops the session from the global `_oauth_sessions` dict — it never signals the background worker (`_codex_full_login_worker`) in any way.

The worker (`hermes_cli/web_server.py`):
- Never re-checks whether the session was cancelled during its poll loop (`hermes_cli/web_server.py:11350-11366`).
- Resolves the *save* profile lazily via `_oauth_session_profile(session_id)` (`hermes_cli/web_server.py:11401-11405`) — **after** polling/exchange completes.

Once the session is popped, `_oauth_session_profile(session_id)` returns `None`, and `_profile_scope(None)` falls back to the **caller's current active profile** — not the profile the login was originally started in.

## Reproduction (deterministic, no network)

1. Start a Codex device-code login for profile `worker`.
2. Call `DELETE /api/providers/oauth/sessions/{session_id}` → `200 OK`, session removed from `_oauth_sessions`.
3. Let the worker's poll succeed anyway (simulating the user approving after cancelling).

Observed:
```text
cancel_http = 200 {'ok': True}
worker_finished = True
session_still_present = False
profile_scope_args = [None]
saved_calls = 1
```
The worker finished authentication and called `_save_codex_tokens()` once, with the original `worker` profile lost — the write falls back to whatever profile happens to be active at that moment.

## Impact

- Violates the user's expectation that "Cancel" aborts the login.
- Can write Codex OAuth credentials into a profile the user never intended (cross-profile credential contamination).
- Cancelled flows keep polling OpenAI for up to their 15-minute expiry window, wasting a thread and HTTP requests.

## Fix

See PR (branch `fix/codex-oauth-cancel-race-ia01`):

- `cancel_oauth_session` now sets `sess["cancelled"] = True` on the shared session dict **before** popping it, so any worker still holding a reference to that same dict object observes the cancellation.
- `_codex_full_login_worker` captures `session_profile = sess.get("profile")` **once**, immediately after publishing the `user_code` — it is never re-derived later, so a cancelled/popped session can no longer fall back to the caller's current profile scope.
- The worker checks `sess.get("cancelled")` before/after each poll sleep, before the authorization-code exchange, and immediately before calling `_save_codex_tokens()` — it returns early at the first check that observes cancellation, skipping the save entirely.

## Tests

Two new regression tests in `tests/hermes_cli/test_web_oauth_dispatch.py`:
- `test_codex_dashboard_worker_stops_polling_after_cancel`
- `test_cancel_oauth_session_marks_dict_cancelled_before_popping`

Full suite: 26/26 passing.

items.title: [Bug] SSH backend fails on Windows: getsockname failed (ControlMaster unsupported)

labels.name: duplicate
labels.description: This issue or pull request already exists

labels.name: sweeper:risk-platform-windows
labels.description: Sweeper risk: may break or behave differently on native Windows

items.body:
## Bug Description

The SSH terminal backend (`tools/environments/ssh.py`) unconditionally adds ControlMaster options to every SSH command, which fails on Windows because Windows OpenSSH does not support Unix-domain ControlMaster sockets.

## Error Message

```
SSH connection failed: getsockname failed: Not a socket
Read from remote host <host>: Unknown error
```

## Reproduction Steps

1. On Windows 10/11, configure a profile with `terminal.backend: ssh`
2. Set `ssh_host`, `ssh_user`, `ssh_key` to a valid remote server
3. Start a new session and run any terminal command
4. All tool calls (terminal, read_file, write_file, etc.) fail with the above error

## Root Cause

`_build_ssh_command()` in `tools/environments/ssh.py` (line 83-98) always appends:

```python
cmd.extend(["-o", f"ControlPath={self.control_socket}"])
cmd.extend(["-o", "ControlMaster=auto"])
cmd.extend(["-o", "ControlPersist=300"])
```

Windows OpenSSH does not support ControlMaster (Unix domain sockets). This causes immediate connection failure.

## Suggested Fix

Wrap the ControlMaster options in an OS check:

```python
if os.name != "nt":
    cmd.extend(["-o", f"ControlPath={self.control_socket}"])
    cmd.extend(["-o", "ControlMaster=auto"])
    cmd.extend(["-o", "ControlPersist=300"])
```

`os` is already imported in the file. This preserves ControlMaster connection reuse on Linux/macOS while allowing the SSH backend to function on Windows (without connection pooling).

## Environment

- OS: Windows 10
- Hermes: v0.19.0 (git install)
- Python: 3.11.15
- SSH client: Windows OpenSSH
- File introduced in commit `ceaa7880e` (2026-07-28)

items.title: [Bug]: Gateway agent:end hooks omit turn exit reason and API call count
items.body:
### What happened?

The Gateway agent:end lifecycle hook receives the response text but not the structured turn termination metadata that run_agent already returns.

On current main 158e9a99779428245c7f524aade8ab398e44676c, gateway/run.py emits agent:end with response only. As a result, a hook cannot distinguish a normal text_response finish from max_iterations_reached, guardrail_halt, retry exhaustion, or user interruption when the response itself looks substantive.

The related open PR #31023 forwards turn_exit_reason through a different gateway result-summary path. It does not add the fields to the agent:end hook context, so this report is not a duplicate of that change.

### Reproduction

1. Register an agent:end hook that records only metadata.
2. Run a turn whose agent result contains turn_exit_reason=max_iterations_reached and a nonzero API call count.
3. Observe that the hook context contains response but neither turn_exit_reason nor api_call_count.

### Expected behavior

The agent:end hook context should additively include:

- turn_exit_reason from the agent result
- api_call_count from the agent result

Existing response-only consumers must continue to work unchanged. A user interruption should remain distinguishable from actionable abnormal exits so downstream policy can classify it as non-actionable.

### Acceptance criteria

- Focused tests cover normal text response, max iterations, guardrail halt, retry exhaustion, and user interruption.
- The fields are emitted once per completed Gateway turn with stable types.
- Hook failures do not change turn delivery behavior.
- No message content, credential, or user PII is added to the new metadata.

### Lineage

correlation_id: hermes-governed-autonomy-rel-01
stable failure class: silent_abnormal_turn_exit

items.title: [Bug]: PowerShell wrapper on Windows produces error noise on every terminal command

labels.name: sweeper:cannot-reproduce
labels.description: Sweeper: could not reproduce on current main

labels.name: sweeper:risk-platform-windows
labels.description: Sweeper risk: may break or behave differently on native Windows

items.body:
---
title: "[Bug]: PowerShell wrapper on Windows: TreatControlCAsInput error on every command + redundant pwsh_transform layer"
labels: ["platform/windows", "tool/terminal", "type/bug", "P3 Low — cosmetic or minor inconvenience"]
---

## Bug Description

On native Windows (PowerShell 5.1 Desktop Edition), every `terminal()` tool invocation is wrapped in a PowerShell command string that produces two classes of noise on **every** command:

### Problem 1: `TreatControlCAsInput` always fails

The wrapper includes:
```powershell
[Console]::TreatControlCAsInput=$true
```

Since the subprocess is spawned via `powershell.exe -NoP -Exec Bypass -NoL -C "..."`, there is no real console handle attached. This causes:
```
Exception setting "TreatControlCAsInput": "The handle is invalid."
```
on **every single command**, producing 2 lines of error output before any actual command output.

### Problem 2: Duplicated wrapper code

The encoding and `TreatControlCAsInput` settings appear **twice** in the constructed wrapper string, doubling the error noise.

### Problem 3: `pwsh_transform` compatibility layer with warnings

Since the runtime binary hardcodes `powershell.exe` (PS5.1) as the outer shell, but the agent (and user) naturally writes PS7 syntax (`&&`, `||`, `??`, `?.`), a `pwsh_transform` layer rewrites PS7 → PS5.1 syntax. This works correctly but emits `pwsh_warnings` metadata on every transformed command, adding noise.

### Problem 4: Binary hardcodes PS5.1

The runtime binary (`hermes-agent-cn-runtime-win32-x64.exe` or equivalent) hardcodes `powershell.exe` path. Even when `pwsh` (PowerShell 7) is installed and available on PATH, the wrapper still routes through PS5.1.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Run Hermes on native Windows (PowerShell 5.1)
2. Execute any terminal command (e.g., `echo "test"`)
3. Observe the output: 2 lines of `TreatControlCAsInput` error before the actual result
4. Execute a command with `&&` (e.g., `echo "a" && echo "b"`)
5. Observe `pwsh_warnings` metadata in the response

## Expected Behavior

1. **No error noise**: `TreatControlCAsInput` should either be skipped on Windows subprocess spawns (no console handle) or wrapped in a try/catch
2. **No duplicate wrapper code**: The encoding/settings should be set once, not twice
3. **Auto-detect pwsh**: If PowerShell 7 (`pwsh`) is available, use it instead of PowerShell 5.1 — this eliminates the need for `pwsh_transform` entirely since PS7 natively supports `&&`/`||`/`??`/`?.`
4. **Silent compatibility**: If PS5.1 must be used, the `pwsh_transform` should not emit warnings for routine syntax transforms

## Actual Behavior

Every terminal command is polluted with:
- 2 lines of `TreatControlCAsInput` errors
- `pwsh_warnings` for PS7 syntax features

## Affected Component

- Tools (terminal)

## Operating System

- Windows 11

## Additional Context

Root cause: the PowerShell wrapper is compiled into the runtime binary (Go/Rust layer), not in the Python `tools/` code. The Python `LocalEnvironment._run_bash()` already supports Git Bash on Windows via `_find_bash()`, but the runtime binary's terminal execution path bypasses this and goes directly through `powershell.exe`.

The wrapper string observed in practice:
```
powershell.exe -NoP -Exec Bypass -NoL -C "
[Console]::OutputEncoding=[System.Text.Encoding]::UTF8;
$OutputEncoding=[System.Text.Encoding]::UTF8;
[Console]::TreatControlCAsInput=$true;           ← fails, no console handle
[Console]::OutputEncoding=[System.Text.Encoding]::UTF8;  ← duplicated
$OutputEncoding=[System.Text.Encoding]::UTF8;            ← duplicated
[Console]::TreatControlCAsInput=$true;                   ← duplicated, fails again
...
Invoke-Expression '<user command>'
...
"
```

items.title: One-shot cron jobs can get permanently stuck when claim_dispatch() increments completed before execution completes

labels.name: P1
labels.description: High — major feature broken, no workaround

labels.name: needs-decision
labels.description: Awaiting maintainer decision before any implementation

items.body:
## Description

One-shot cron jobs (repeat.times=1) can enter a wedged state where `repeat.completed` is incremented to 1 (== times) but `last_run_at` stays null, no output file is created, and the job remains in `state: "scheduled"` forever. The job is then unrecoverable — the run_claim TTL prevents re-dispatch, and once the TTL expires the dispatch-limit guard removes the job without producing any output.

## Evidence

A concrete instance was observed on a scheduled one-shot job:

```
"repeat":     { "times": 1, "completed": 1 },   ← consumed
"run_claim":  { "at": "2026-07-29T09:33:13", "by": "BlueGene:13328" },
"state":      "scheduled",                      ← never transitioned
"last_run_at": null,                            ← never set
```

The desktop app log shows the cron scheduler restarted at 09:30:02 — the exact scheduled fire time — likely killing the previous ticker process mid-execution:

```
2026-07-29 09:30:02,771 INFO hermes_cli.web_server: Desktop cron scheduler started (provider=builtin, interval=60s)
```

No output directory was created under `cron/output/{job_id}/`.

## Root Cause Analysis

### The chain of events

The execution pipeline in `cron/scheduler.py:run_one_job()` is:

1. **`claim_dispatch(job["id"])`** (jobs.py:1743) — **increments `repeat.completed` BEFORE execution** (by design, at-most-times semantics). This persists the claim under the file lock so a tick that dies mid-execution cannot re-fire the job infinitely.

2. **`run_job()`** — executes the agent (creates AIAgent, runs conversation, waits for result).

3. **`mark_job_run(job["id"], success, error)`** — on success or caught Exception, sets `last_run_at`, clears `run_claim`, and transitions state.

### The bug

If something prevents `mark_job_run()` from being called _after_ `claim_dispatch()` succeeded, the job is left with `completed` already consumed but `last_run_at` never written:

```
claim_dispatch() → completed: 0 → 1   ✓ persisted
run_job()         → ... fails ...
mark_job_run()    → NEVER CALLED       ✗
```

In `run_one_job()` (scheduler.py:3880-4036), the outer exception handler at line 4031 catches only `Exception`, **not** `BaseException`:

```python
except Exception as e:           # ← DOES NOT catch BaseException!
    mark_job_run(job["id"], False, str(e))
```

But the inner handler at line 3950 catches `BaseException` (which includes `asyncio.CancelledError`, `KeyboardInterrupt`, `SystemExit`) and **re-raises** it after teardown. When the re-raised exception propagates to the outer handler, it is NOT caught by `except Exception` — so `mark_job_run()` is never called.

In Python 3.14:
```python
>>> issubclass(asyncio.CancelledError, Exception)
False
>>> issubclass(asyncio.CancelledError, BaseException)
True
```

### Why this specifically manifests on the desktop app

The desktop app runs its own cron ticker (`hermes_cli.web_server: Desktop cron scheduler started`). When the desktop app restarts (e.g., at the exact fire time of the scheduled job, as seen in the logs), the old ticker process is killed mid-flight. The sequence becomes:

1. Old process ticks → gets due job → stamps `run_claim` → `claim_dispatch()` increments `completed` → starts `run_job()` → **process killed** (app restart)
2. New process starts → ticker initializes → next tick finds job with `completed=1, last_run_at=null` → fresh `run_claim` blocks re-dispatch for TTL (default 30 min) → job stuck
3. After TTL expires → `get_due_jobs()` dispatch-limit guard (jobs.py:2210) sees `completed >= times` → **removes the job silently** — no output, no error, no user-facing alert

Additionally, the `cronjob action=run` tool also removes one-shot jobs when `completed >= times`, making manual recovery impossible.

## Affected Components

- `cron/jobs.py` — `claim_dispatch()` (line 1743) increments completed before execution
- `cron/scheduler.py` — `run_one_job()` (line 4031) `except Exception` misses `BaseException`
- `cron/scheduler.py` — `get_due_jobs()` dispatch-limit guard silently removes stuck jobs

## Suggested Fix

Two complementary approaches:

1. **Safe:** Change the outer `except Exception` in `run_one_job()` to `except BaseException` so `mark_job_run(False)` is called even on `CancelledError`/`KeyboardInterrupt`/`SystemExit`:

```python
except BaseException as e:
    if not _consume_interrupted_flag(job["id"]):
        mark_job_run(job["id"], False, str(e))
    finish_execution(execution_id, success=False, error=str(e))
    if not isinstance(e, Exception):
        raise  # re-raise non-Exception BaseExceptions after recording the failure
    return False
```

2. **Defense-in-depth:** In `get_due_jobs()`, when the dispatch-limit guard removes a one-shot that has `completed >= times` but no `last_run_at`, write a diagnostic file to the output directory instead of removing silently, so the operator can see what happened.

## Workaround

Manually firing the job via `cronjob action=run` does NOT help — it also removes the job without running it. The only recovery is to recreate the job.

items.title: [Bug]: run_gateway() os._exit(0) kills the pytest process in test_run_gateway_refreshes_outdated_unit_on_boot — file reported ✓ with all its tests silently dropped

labels.name: duplicate
labels.description: This issue or pull request already exists

labels.name: comp/cli
labels.description: CLI entry point, hermes_cli/, setup wizard

labels.name: sweeper:risk-message-delivery
labels.description: Sweeper risk: may drop, duplicate, misroute, or suppress messages

items.body:
## Summary

`tests/hermes_cli/test_gateway_service.py::TestSystemdServiceRefresh::test_run_gateway_refreshes_outdated_unit_on_boot` terminates the pytest process via `os._exit(0)` before its assertions run. The process exits **0 with zero bytes of output**, so `scripts/run_tests_parallel.py` marks the file `✓` while every test in it is silently dropped from the totals.

## Reproduction

```console
$ python -m pytest -q "tests/hermes_cli/test_gateway_service.py::TestSystemdServiceRefresh::test_run_gateway_refreshes_outdated_unit_on_boot" > out.txt 2>&1
$ echo $?
0
$ wc -c < out.txt
0
```

No summary line, no traceback, no collection output — the interpreter is gone before pytest can report anything.

## Root cause

The test stubs `gateway.run.start_gateway` so that `run_gateway()` reaches its clean-success path:

```python
# hermes_cli/gateway.py:5063
_exit_diag("gateway.exit_clean")
_hard_exit_after_gateway_teardown(0)
```

`_hard_exit_after_gateway_teardown` imports `_exit_after_graceful_shutdown` from `gateway.run` **inside the function body**, so the test's `monkeypatch` of `gateway.run.start_gateway` does not cover it. That helper ends in an unconditional hard exit:

```python
# gateway/run.py:25016
os._exit(exit_code)
```

Consequently the assertions the test was written to make are unreachable:

```python
# tests/hermes_cli/test_gateway_service.py:242-245
gateway_cli.run_gateway()

assert unit_path.read_text(encoding="utf-8") == "new unit\n"     # never evaluated
assert ["systemctl", "--user", "daemon-reload"] in calls          # never evaluated
```

## Impact on the parallel runner

`scripts/run_tests_parallel.py` derives per-file status from the return code (`status = "✓" if rc == 0 else "✗"`) and parses counts from pytest's summary line, which is absent here. The `NO TESTS RAN` guard only fires when the **global** collected total is zero, so it is silenced by any healthy file in the same run:

```console
$ python scripts/run_tests_parallel.py tests/hermes_cli/test_gateway_service.py tests/acp/test_auth.py
✓ tests/hermes_cli/test_gateway_service.py (189 tests, 0.4s)
✓ tests/acp/test_auth.py (10✓, 1.8s)
=== Summary: 2 files, 10 tests passed, 0 failed (100% complete) in 1.8s (48 workers) ===
```

The file is reported green and advertised as "189 tests", yet contributes **0** to the totals. In a full-suite run those 189 tests are silently skipped and the suite still reports success.

Run alone, the file *is* caught (`✗ NO TESTS RAN — 0 collected across 1 file`), which is why this does not surface in single-file debugging.

## Suggested directions

- Patch the exit path in the test (e.g. `monkeypatch.setattr("gateway.run._exit_after_graceful_shutdown", lambda code: None)`), or have `run_gateway()` return instead of hard-exiting when the gateway was stubbed out.
- Independently, consider treating "subprocess exited 0 but reported no summary line" as a per-file failure in `run_tests_parallel.py`. That would turn this whole class of silent test loss into a loud one, regardless of which test causes it.

## Environment

| | |
|---|---|
| hermes-agent | 0.19.0 |
| commit | `ceaa7880e` (`v2026.7.20-2503-gceaa7880e`) |
| Python | 3.11.15 |
| pytest | 9.0.2 (pytest-asyncio 1.3.0) |
| OS | Linux x86_64 |

Reproduced on an unmodified checkout of the affected paths (`hermes_cli/`, `gateway/`, `tests/`).

items.title: [Feature]: Expose Kanban worker session ID and token usage in run API

labels.name: needs-decision
labels.description: Awaiting maintainer decision before any implementation

labels.name: comp/dashboard
labels.description: Web dashboard / control panel UI (dashboard/, landing)

labels.name: area/usage-cost
labels.description: Token accounting, usage reporting, billing, cost tracking

items.body:
## Problem or Use Case

Hermes Kanban exposes task and run state, but external orchestrators cannot reliably attribute a Kanban run to the Hermes worker session that executed it.

This makes per-task observability difficult. In particular, an integration cannot accurately retrieve:

- the worker session ID for a Kanban run;
- input/output/cache/reasoning token usage for that run;
- usage across retries or child sessions;
- cost or quota attribution per task.

Today, integrations have to use fragile workarounds such as parsing worker logs, searching SessionDB message content for task IDs, or matching sessions by timestamps and profile.

This is especially problematic for systems using Hermes as a managed execution backend, where a durable mapping is needed:

```text
Kanban task -> Kanban run -> Hermes worker session -> token usage
```

## Proposed Solution

Expose the worker session ID as a first-class field on every Kanban run and include it in the Kanban Dashboard/API response.

Example:

```json
{
  "id": "run_123",
  "task_id": "task_123",
  "status": "done",
  "worker_session_id": "session_abc",
  "usage": {
    "input_tokens": 120000,
    "cached_input_tokens": 108000,
    "cache_write_tokens": 0,
    "output_tokens": 18000,
    "reasoning_tokens": 4000,
    "total_tokens": 138000,
    "updated_at": "2026-07-29T08:00:00Z"
  }
}
```

The minimum useful change would be only:

```json
{
  "worker_session_id": "session_abc"
}
```

With that stable mapping, external systems can read usage from SessionDB themselves without requiring Hermes to duplicate usage accounting in Kanban.

## Suggested Behavior

- Persist `worker_session_id` when the worker session is created, not only when `kanban_complete` or `kanban_block` is called.
- Preserve the mapping when a worker crashes, times out, or is killed.
- Ensure concurrent workers cannot inherit or overwrite another worker's session ID.
- If compression or continuation creates child sessions, expose either:
  - the root worker session ID plus lineage information; or
  - all session IDs associated with the run.
- Treat token usage as optional so providers without detailed usage can return `null`.

## API Surface

Suggested endpoints to extend:

```http
GET /api/plugins/kanban/tasks/:id
GET /api/plugins/kanban/runs/:id
```

Suggested fields:

```text
worker_session_id: string | null
worker_session_ids: string[] | null
usage: object | null
```

## Why This Should Be Separate From a Larger Managed Runtime Feature

This overlaps with the broader managed runtime / observability direction discussed in #26675, but this request is intentionally small and independently useful.

A stable `Kanban run -> worker session` mapping alone removes most of the need for brittle log and SessionDB heuristics, while leaving token aggregation and cost accounting optional.

## Related Issue

#65407 notes that `tools/kanban_tools.py` stamps the worker session ID from session environment state and identifies correctness risks under concurrency. That suggests some of the internal plumbing already exists, but it is not currently a stable persisted/API contract.

## Alternatives Considered

1. Search SessionDB messages for the Kanban task ID.
2. Match sessions using run timestamps, profile, and task text.
3. Parse Kanban worker log paths.
4. Modify Hermes locally to add custom metadata.

All are more fragile than exposing the runtime identity Hermes already owns.

## Expected Benefit

This would enable accurate per-task usage dashboards, retry accounting, capacity planning, billing, and external orchestration without requiring downstream projects to fork Hermes or depend on internal database layouts.

items.title: WebUI: Display Active LLM Model, Including Fallbacks, Not Just Configured Default

labels.name: duplicate
labels.description: This issue or pull request already exists

labels.name: comp/dashboard
labels.description: Web dashboard / control panel UI (dashboard/, landing)

items.body:
### Problem

The Hermes WebUI currently displays the configured default LLM model (sourced from `config.yaml` via `/api/session-status`'s `config.model` or `contextUsage.model`). This is problematic when the configured model fails and a fallback model is silently used by the Hermes gateway or the platform running the WebUI.

For example, if `config.yaml` specifies `model: custom:LongCat-2.0`, the WebUI will show "LongCat 2.0". However, if `LongCat-2.0` is unavailable or fails, and the system transparently falls back to `gemini-2.5-flash` to process a user's prompt, the WebUI continues to display "LongCat 2.0".

This discrepancy leads to user confusion, as the displayed model does not accurately reflect the model actively processing their requests.

### Desired Behavior

The WebUI should consistently display the *actual, live LLM model* that is currently processing the user's conversational turns. If a fallback mechanism is engaged, the name of the active fallback model should be shown instead of, or in addition to, the originally configured model.

### Impact

- **User Confusion**: Users are misled into believing they are interacting with a specific model, which can lead to incorrect expectations about performance, cost, and specific model capabilities.
- **Debugging Difficulty**: When issues arise, it is harder for users to diagnose problems or provide accurate feedback if they do not know which model is truly at play.
- **Misaligned Workflow**: Developers or users creating specific workflows (e.g., for PR review companions) might configure a model with certain traits but unknowingly have their tasks processed by a different, potentially less suitable, fallback model.

### Technical Context

The `chat-screen.tsx` (line ~1000-1061) shows the model by querying `GET /api/session-status`. The API (`session-status.ts`) resolves the model as `session.model ?? config.model ?? contextUsage.model`. When the session has no active run (e.g., new session or before first message), it falls to `config.model` -- the static YAML value -- regardless of what model actually processes the next request.

The fallback resolution (e.g., via `fallback_providers` or gateway-level model routing) is never propagated back into the API response.

### Code References

- **`hermes-workspace/src/screens/chat/chat-screen.tsx`**: Lines ~1000-1061: `currentModelQuery` fetches from session-status, resolves model.
- **`hermes-workspace/src/routes/api/session-status.ts`**: Lines ~172-178: Resolution of `session.model ?? config.model`.
- **`hermes-workspace/src/server/context-usage.ts`**: Lines ~207-230: `readConfiguredModelContext()` fetches model from dashboard API.
- **`hermes-workspace/src/lib/format-model-name.ts`**: Display formatting for model names.

### Proposed Approach (do not implement)

Consider adding a field to the `/api/session-status` response payload, such as `activeModel` or `fallbackModel`, that reflects the model actually being used for the current session, distinct from the configured default. The WebUI would then source its model indicator from this field. Alternatively, the gateway runtime snapshot (`/api/sessions/:id/runtime`) could be enhanced to report the active model.

items.title: Context compaction permanently poisons sessions on Mistral-template backends (summary emitted as role:user after a tool-flow head)

labels.name: comp/agent
labels.description: Core agent runtime: loop, agent_init, prompt builder, context-compression, responses endpoint

labels.name: P1
labels.description: High — major feature broken, no workaround

labels.name: sweeper:risk-session-state
labels.description: Sweeper risk: may lose/corrupt/mis-associate session or context state

items.body:
## Bug Description

Every context compaction against a Mistral-family model served by llama.cpp
(Devstral, Mistral Small 3.x, Magistral - anything using Mistral's strict chat
template) kills the session permanently with:

```
HTTP 500: Jinja Exception: After the optional system message, conversation
roles must alternate user and assistant roles except for tool calls and results
```

The malformed history is persisted in the stored conversation and re-sent
verbatim on every retry (we captured three byte-identical requests in a row),
so the session never recovers. This fires on EVERY compaction, not only after
a context overflow.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Point a custom OpenAI-compatible provider at llama.cpp/llama-swap serving
   `Devstral-Small-2-24B` (or any Mistral-template model), compression enabled.
2. Run any tool-heavy task long enough to cross the compression threshold
   (e.g. "run a full systems diagnostics").
3. The first compaction produces the 500 above; every subsequent turn repeats
   it byte-identically.

## Root Cause

Captured byte-exact with a tee-proxy between Hermes Desktop v0.19.0 and
llama-swap. Head of the compacted request:

```
[0] system     (system prompt)
[1] user       (original first user turn, protected)
[2] assistant  tool_calls=[...], content=""
[3] tool       "[terminal] ran ... -> exit 127"
[4] user       "[CONTEXT COMPACTION - REFERENCE ONLY] ..."   <- the summary
[5..] assistant(tool_calls)/tool pairs only
```

In `agent/context_compressor.py`, summary-role selection reads the LITERAL
neighbouring roles (`compressed[-1]` / `tail_messages[0]`). Here the literal
previous role is `tool`, so the summary is pinned to `role="user"`.

But Mistral's template exempts the tool flow (`tool` messages and assistant
messages carrying `tool_calls`) from its alternation check. The last role the
template actually counts is the user at [1], the next is the summary at [4]:
user -> user, and the template raises at render time, rejecting the entire
request.

The role pinning itself is intentional (#52160 Anthropic user-first, #58753
zero-user-turn guard) - the bug is only that neighbour roles are computed
literally instead of as the template counts them.

## Expected Behavior

The summary role should alternate against the nearest TEMPLATE-VISIBLE
neighbours (skipping tool results and assistant tool-call messages). For the
captured shape that means `role="assistant"`, which we verified renders and
generates cleanly: replaying the captured poisoned request with only that one
role flipped turns the 500 into a normal streaming completion.

Both forced-user guards are unaffected: their shapes (summary-user followed
only by template-exempt messages) already satisfy the alternation check.

## Environment

- Hermes Agent v0.19.0 (2026.7.20), Desktop, Windows 11
- Provider: custom OpenAI-compatible (llama-swap -> llama.cpp b1366-2969d6d1)
- Model: Devstral-Small-2-24B (UD-Q5_K_XL), 64k ctx
- Compression: defaults (enabled, threshold 0.50), explicit context length
  64000 configured

I have a fix with regression tests ready and will open a PR referencing this
issue.
