labels.name: sweeper:risk-compatibility
labels.description: Sweeper risk: may break existing users, config, migrations, defaults, or upgrades

items.body:
## Summary
`resolve_entry_api_key()` reads `key_env` directly from the process environment with `os.getenv()`. In a multiplexed gateway (multiple profiles/accounts sharing one process), this bypasses per-profile secret scoping and can select another profile's credential for a fallback request.

## Root cause
- `hermes_cli/fallback_config.py`, `resolve_entry_api_key()` (lines 15-31): `return os.getenv(key_env, "").strip() or None` — reads the raw process environment, ignoring any active secret scope.
- `agent/secret_scope.py`'s `get_secret()` (~lines 123-177) is the contract meant to isolate secrets per profile and fail closed under multiplexing — but it isn't used here.
- Every caller of `resolve_entry_api_key()` inherits the bug: `hermes_cli/cli_agent_setup_mixin.py` (~lines 49-68), `gateway/run.py` (~lines 2449-2459), `cron/scheduler.py` (~lines 3330-3349) — none re-scope the result afterward.
- `agent/auxiliary_client.py` (~lines 4724-4732) duplicates the same raw `os.getenv()` pattern independently.

## Impact
- Breaks credential isolation between profiles.
- CLI, gateway, cron, and auxiliary-task fallback requests can use the wrong account's key.
- Can leak one profile's credential to the endpoint configured under a different active profile.
- Cost/usage/rate-limit accounting can be attributed to the wrong account.

## Suggested fix (root cause)
Resolve `key_env` through `secret_scope.get_secret()` on every multiplexable call path, keeping `os.getenv()` only as an explicit fallback outside of an active multiplexed scope where the contract allows it. Centralize this in one function (used by all four callers above) instead of duplicating the raw env lookup, and add a regression test with two profiles and divergent sentinel values.

## Reproduction
Unit test with the active secret scope holding `fake-active-profile-key` and `os.environ` holding a different `fake-other-profile-key`. `resolve_entry_api_key()` returns the environment value (`fake-other-profile-key`) instead of the scoped one.

items.title: routing: substring "azure.com" match on full base URL misclassifies non-Azure host, picks wrong credential

labels.name: comp/cli
labels.description: CLI entry point, hermes_cli/, setup wizard

labels.name: sweeper:risk-security-boundary
labels.description: Sweeper risk: may affect sandboxing, auth, credentials, or sensitive data

items.body:
## Summary
A URL whose **path** (not hostname) contains the text `azure.com` is classified as an Azure endpoint, even when the actual host is not Azure. This causes the wrong routing/credential (Azure key instead of the explicit Anthropic token) to be selected.

## Root cause
- `hermes_cli/runtime_provider.py` line ~1682: `if requested_provider == "anthropic" and "azure.com" in _eff_base:` — a raw substring test against the full effective base URL string (path, query, userinfo included), not a parsed hostname check.
- The same pattern is duplicated at ~lines 2022-2023: `"azure.com" in base_url.lower() or (cfg_base_url and "azure.com" in cfg_base_url.lower())`.
- The codebase already has a correct hostname-boundary helper (`base_url_host_matches()`, used correctly elsewhere, e.g. lines ~1054, 1113, 1239, and the `.endswith(".azure.com")` check at ~line 247) — it just isn't used at these two sites.

## Impact
- Sends the wrong credential to a non-Azure host (e.g. a proxy/custom endpoint whose path happens to contain `azure.com`).
- Breaks the legitimate Anthropic route with an authentication failure.
- In proxy/custom-endpoint configurations, a more-privileged Azure key can cross a trust boundary it shouldn't.

## Suggested fix (root cause)
Parse the URL and validate only the hostname against allowed Azure suffixes, with proper boundary rules (`host == domain` or `host.endswith("." + domain)`) — never classify by substring presence in path/query/userinfo. Apply the existing `base_url_host_matches()` helper at both sites (~1682 and ~2022-2023) instead of the raw substring checks.

## Reproduction
Unit test, no network: base URL `https://example.invalid/proxy/azure.com/v1`, sentinel Anthropic token, sentinel Azure key. Result: the resolver selects the Azure credential/route instead of the explicit Anthropic one, purely because of the path text.

items.title: codex: dict-shaped usage silently normalizes to zero (getattr on a mapping)

labels.name: comp/agent
labels.description: Core agent runtime: loop, agent_init, prompt builder, context-compression, responses endpoint

labels.name: area/usage-cost
labels.description: Token accounting, usage reporting, billing, cost tracking

items.body:
## Summary
The Codex Responses terminal-event handler accepts a plain-`dict` shaped response and keeps `usage` as a raw mapping. The shared usage normalizer only reads via `getattr()`, so every field — including nested cache/reasoning detail counts — silently comes back as zero for a dict.

## Root cause
- `agent/codex_runtime.py` (~lines 1157-1188): when the terminal response object is a `dict`, `terminal_usage = resp_obj.get("usage")` is stored as-is (a plain mapping), not converted to an attribute-style object.
- `agent/usage_pricing.py`'s `normalize_usage()` (~lines 1205-1291) reads exclusively via `getattr(response_usage, "input_tokens", 0)` etc., including for nested `input_tokens_details` / `output_tokens_details` (~lines 1236, 1281).
- `getattr({...}, "input_tokens", 0)` on a plain `dict` returns the default (`0`) rather than raising, since dicts don't expose attribute access — so the failure is silent.
- Note: this is distinct from the app-server dict path (`codex_runtime.py` ~lines 46-110, `_record_codex_app_server_usage`), which already correctly uses `.get()` — the bug is specific to the raw Responses-API terminal-event path.

## Impact
- Token counts and cost appear as zero whenever Relay/middleware/backend returns plain JSON (dict) instead of a typed SDK object.
- Cache hit-rate metrics become incorrect.
- `ContextCompressor.update_from_response()` receives zeroed usage, which can delay triggering compression.
- Any post-request hook relying on usage gets false metrics.

## Suggested fix (root cause)
Use a common accessor that supports both attribute objects and `Mapping` at every level, including the nested cache/reasoning detail objects. Add a contract test that feeds the same payload as both a typed object and an equivalent dict, and asserts identical normalized output.

## Reproduction
Input: `{"input_tokens": 100, "output_tokens": 20, "input_tokens_details": {"cached_tokens": 60}, "output_tokens_details": {"reasoning_tokens": 7}}`. Output from `normalize_usage`: `input_tokens=0, output_tokens=0, cache_read_tokens=0, reasoning_tokens=0` — all zeroed despite valid data.

items.title: api: negative limit query params bypass pagination clamps on session/message routes

labels.name: comp/cli
labels.description: CLI entry point, hermes_cli/, setup wizard

labels.name: sweeper:risk-session-state
labels.description: Sweeper risk: may lose/corrupt/mis-associate session or context state

labels.name: comp/dashboard
labels.description: Web dashboard / control panel UI (dashboard/, landing)

items.body:
## Summary
Negative `limit` values are accepted by three session-related routes and passed straight through to SQLite `LIMIT` clauses, where `LIMIT -1` means "no limit". This bypasses both the default page size and the documented 500-message clamp.

## Root cause
- `GET /api/sessions` (`hermes_cli/web_server.py`, `limit: int = 20`, ~line 4728): no lower bound (`Query(ge=0)` or clamp) on `limit`/`offset`.
- `GET /api/profiles/sessions` (~line 4841 signature, clamp computed ~line 4898): `per_profile = min(max(limit + offset, limit), 500)` — for `limit=-1, offset=0`, this evaluates to `-1`, unbounded per profile.
- `GET /api/sessions/{id}/messages` (~lines 11866-11881): `_limit = min(limit, 500) if limit is not None else None` — `min(-1, 500)` is `-1`, so the "clamped to 500" guarantee is trivially bypassed.
- Both `hermes_state.py`'s `get_messages` (~lines 5580-5612) and the `list_sessions_rich` query (~lines 6280-6288) build `LIMIT ? OFFSET ?` directly from these values with no `max(0, ...)` anywhere in the chain.

## Impact
- An authenticated client can force large/unbounded responses and repeated full reads.
- `full=1` amplifies cost further by including full prompts/config per session.
- Can raise memory, CPU, I/O, and dashboard/backend traffic.
- The messages endpoint claims a 500-row clamp that is trivially bypassed.

## Suggested fix (root cause)
Validate at the FastAPI layer with `Query(ge=0, le=500)` (or an explicit `max(0, min(limit, 500))` clamp) on all three routes, applied consistently, and also bound `offset` to `>= 0`.

## Note
Distinct from #69640 (desktop loads the entire active transcript, no incremental pagination) — that issue is about missing pagination when `limit` is omitted; this one is about negative values bypassing pagination that clients *do* pass correctly.

## Reproduction
Real SQLite DB with 600 messages / 31 sessions. `limit=500` → 500 rows (correct). `limit=-1` → 600 rows (all of them) on the messages endpoint, and 31 (all) sessions returned on both the sessions list and profiles/sessions endpoints regardless of their stated defaults/clamps.

items.title: bug(secrets): cold multiplex profiles do not resolve configured external sources into their secret scope

labels.name: comp/agent
labels.description: Core agent runtime: loop, agent_init, prompt builder, context-compression, responses endpoint

labels.name: comp/cli
labels.description: CLI entry point, hermes_cli/, setup wizard

labels.name: needs-decision
labels.description: Awaiting maintainer decision before any implementation

labels.name: sweeper:risk-security-boundary
labels.description: Sweeper risk: may affect sandboxing, auth, credentials, or sensitive data

labels.name: sweeper:risk-compatibility
labels.description: Sweeper risk: may break existing users, config, migrations, defaults, or upgrades

items.body:
## TL;DR

- #69250 correctly made **already-applied** external-secret values visible to the matching profile's multiplex secret scope.
- A secondary profile selected for its **first** routed multiplex turn may never have applied its configured external source in that gateway process, so it has no per-home snapshot to merge and provider initialization fails closed.
- Fix the missing profile-safe source-resolution handoff. Do **not** solve this through root credential inheritance or a raw `os.environ` fallback.

## Bug description

A gateway running with `gateway.multiplex_profiles: true` can route an inbound event to a secondary profile whose provider key is configured through an external source such as 1Password or Bitwarden.

If that profile's external source has not already been applied in the current gateway process, its isolated secret scope does not contain the key. Provider resolution then correctly fails closed with an error such as:

```text
No usable credentials found for provider '<provider>'. Set <PROVIDER>_API_KEY.
```

This is a cold-secondary-profile failure: direct CLI use of the profile can work, and a profile can work after some other path has applied its sources, while its first routed multiplex turn fails.

## Confirmed root cause

`#69250` added per-home snapshots in `hermes_cli.env_loader`:

```text
_apply_external_secret_sources(profile_home)
  -> _SECRET_SOURCE_VALUES_BY_HOME[profile_home]

build_profile_secret_scope(profile_home)
  -> get_secret_source_values(profile_home)
  -> merge snapshot into the active profile scope
```

That protects isolation: a profile scope consumes only values recorded for its own resolved home, not arbitrary process-global environment variables.

However, the secondary multiplex runtime path constructs a scope before it has applied that profile's configured external sources:

```text
Gateway startup
  -> root/default home applies its sources

First event routed to secondary profile
  -> _profile_runtime_scope(profile_home)
  -> build_profile_secret_scope(profile_home)
  -> profile snapshot is empty
  -> scoped provider lookup misses
  -> fail-closed provider initialization error
```

The ordinary dotenv/source loader cannot simply be invoked in this path because it writes resolved profile values into process-global `os.environ`. That would reintroduce the cross-profile credential-leak hazard that multiplex secret scopes were designed to prevent.

## Minimal reproduction

1. Enable `gateway.multiplex_profiles`.
2. Configure the root/default home without `PROVIDER_API_KEY`.
3. Configure a secondary profile with the provider key exclusively through an enabled external secret source.
4. Start the shared gateway without separately invoking the secondary profile in that same process.
5. Send the first inbound event that routes to the secondary profile.

**Actual:** the profile scope is missing the key and provider initialization fails.

**Expected:** the routed profile resolves its own configured external source into its local secret scope, without making that value visible to sibling profiles or global process environment consumers.

## Why this is not already fixed

### Merged foundation: #69250

[#69250](https://github.com/NousResearch/hermes-agent/pull/69250) (`fix(secrets): scope vault-injected keys per profile home`) merged the right isolation primitive:

- immutable external-source snapshots keyed by resolved `HERMES_HOME`;
- same-home snapshot merge in `build_profile_secret_scope()`;
- fail-closed lookup in multiplex mode instead of fallback to another profile's `os.environ` value.

Its regression tests pre-populate the per-home snapshot or apply sources before scope construction. They do not exercise a first routed event for a secondary profile whose configured source has not yet been applied in that process.

[#66342](https://github.com/NousResearch/hermes-agent/pull/66342), later closed as overlapping/superseded work, documented the same snapshot approach. Its review discussion identified this missing source-application handoff for cold secondary profiles.

### Related, but not this fix

| Item | Relationship |
|---|---|
| [#58100](https://github.com/NousResearch/hermes-agent/issues/58100) / [#58111](https://github.com/NousResearch/hermes-agent/pull/58111) | Historical predecessor salvaged by #69250. |
| [#65945](https://github.com/NousResearch/hermes-agent/pull/65945) / [#66182](https://github.com/NousResearch/hermes-agent/pull/66182) | Complementary fail-closed credential-pool hardening. Prevents cross-profile fallback; does not hydrate a valid profile-owned source. |
| [#74265](https://github.com/NousResearch/hermes-agent/issues/74265) / [#74283](https://github.com/NousResearch/hermes-agent/pull/74283) | Protects an already-resolved external value from a later dotenv reload. Compatible but does not resolve a cold secondary profile. |
| [#70652](https://github.com/NousResearch/hermes-agent/issues/70652) / [#69943](https://github.com/NousResearch/hermes-agent/issues/69943) | Adjacent multiplex scope-installation and scope-blind-read gaps. |

### Rejected alternatives

- [#61073](https://github.com/NousResearch/hermes-agent/pull/61073) / [#61094](https://github.com/NousResearch/hermes-agent/pull/61094): inherit root `.env` and root external credentials into named profiles. This changes the trust model and reintroduces root credential sharing.
- [#70616](https://github.com/NousResearch/hermes-agent/pull/70616): layer the default/root home as a credential baseline for every profile. This can mask the symptom but is inappropriate where profiles intentionally have different authority or credential boundaries.
- Raw `os.environ` fallback on a multiplex scope miss: unsafe because process environment values may belong to another profile.

## Proposed direction

Add a profile-safe resolver used before or during `build_profile_secret_scope(profile_home)` that:

1. reads only that profile's configured external secret-source settings;
2. resolves sources into a local mapping, never directly into global `os.environ`;
3. records/reuses the existing per-home snapshot mechanism from #69250;
4. preserves profile `.env` precedence for explicitly defined keys;
5. excludes genuinely global environment variables from the scoped mapping;
6. preserves fail-closed behavior when the routed profile does not own the requested key.

The implementation should reuse the existing source registry rather than introducing a provider-specific 1Password/Bitwarden path.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] A secondary profile with a provider key only in its configured external source completes its **first** routed multiplex turn.
- [ ] The root/default profile does not need to hold that provider key.
- [ ] A sibling profile without the key cannot resolve it.
- [ ] Resolving the secondary profile's source does not write its credentials to global `os.environ`.
- [ ] Explicit values in the profile `.env` retain their documented precedence.
- [ ] Existing #69250 per-home snapshot isolation remains intact.
- [ ] Regression coverage follows the real path: configured source → gateway startup → first event routed to secondary profile → scoped provider credential resolution.

## Scope

This issue is limited to profile-scoped external-source hydration in multiplexed gateway execution. It does not change root/profile inheritance policy, platform adapter configuration, or authorization-gate isolation.

---

*Prepared with AI assistance; code paths and linked prior work were reviewed against current source and GitHub artifacts.*

items.title: routing: persisted model.api_mode from a different provider leaks into explicit-provider resolution

labels.name: comp/cli
labels.description: CLI entry point, hermes_cli/, setup wizard

labels.name: sweeper:risk-compatibility
labels.description: Sweeper risk: may break existing users, config, migrations, defaults, or upgrades

items.body:
## Summary
When explicitly resolving a provider (e.g. via `explicit_api_key`/`explicit_base_url`, such as switching to Gemini), the runtime can inherit a persisted `model.api_mode` left over from a previously configured, different provider — sending requests over an incompatible transport.

## Root cause
- `_resolve_explicit_runtime()` (`hermes_cli/runtime_provider.py`, ~lines 1465-1624), generic-provider branch (~lines 1574-1622): `configured_mode = _parse_api_mode(model_cfg.get("api_mode"))` (~line 1605) is accepted unconditionally whenever truthy (~lines 1606-1607) — with no check that `model_cfg.get("provider")` matches the provider actually being resolved.
- A guard function for exactly this already exists, `_provider_supports_explicit_api_mode(provider, configured_provider)` (~lines 303-317), explicitly documented to prevent "stale api_mode from a previous provider leaking into a different one after a model/provider switch" — but it is only called from the copilot path (~line 328) and a different resolution path (~lines 518, 2201). It is never invoked inside `_resolve_explicit_runtime`'s mode-selection.

## Impact
- Request is sent using the wrong protocol/endpoint for the resolved provider.
- An explicit provider switch can leave the session unusable until the persisted config is fixed manually.
- Fallback/diagnostic logic can misattribute the resulting failure to the wrong provider.

## Suggested fix (root cause)
Only accept a persisted `model.api_mode` when the config's `provider` field matches the provider actually being resolved. Call the existing `_provider_supports_explicit_api_mode()` guard inside `_resolve_explicit_runtime`'s mode-selection block (~line 1605) instead of leaving that path unguarded, and add table-driven tests covering provider-switch transitions.

## Reproduction
Explicit provider `gemini` with fake endpoint/key, but persisted config left over from `anthropic` (`api_mode="anthropic_messages"`). Resolved mode comes back as `anthropic_messages` instead of the correct `chat_completions` for Gemini.

items.title: [Bug]: write_file and patch resolve /opt/data/cache/documents/ to non-existent host path inside Docker container — writes fail silently

labels.name: sweeper:implemented-on-main
labels.description: Sweeper: behavior already present on current main

items.body:
## Summary

When `terminal.backend: docker`, the `write_file` and `patch` tools resolve container paths under `/opt/data/cache/documents/` back to the host filesystem path (`/home/<user>/.hermes/cache/documents/`) before executing the write via `docker exec`. Inside the container, that host path does not exist, so the write fails. The `terminal` tool is unaffected because it passes paths through to the container's shell without resolution.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Run Hermes with `terminal.backend: docker` and the default volume mounts (which include `/home/<user>/.hermes/cache/documents` mounted at both `/opt/data/cache/documents` and `/output` inside the container).
2. Create a file via terminal:
   ```bash
   echo "hello" > /opt/data/cache/documents/test.txt
   ```
3. Attempt to overwrite via `write_file`:
   ```
   write_file(path="/opt/data/cache/documents/test.txt", content="world")
   ```
4. Observe the error.

## Expected Behavior

`write_file` and `patch` should write successfully to `/opt/data/cache/documents/test.txt`, since that path exists and is writable inside the container (rw mount).

## Actual Behavior

```
write_file(path="/opt/data/cache/documents/test.txt", content="world")
→ error: "Failed to write file: bash: line 3: /home/<user>/.hermes/cache/documents/.hermes-tmp.NNNN: No such file or directory"
  resolved_path: "/home/<user>/.hermes/cache/documents/test.txt"
  bytes_written: 0
```

The tool resolves `/opt/data/cache/documents/` to `/home/<user>/.hermes/cache/documents/` (the host path) and attempts to write there. Inside the container, `/home/<user>/` does not exist:
```
$ ls -la /home/<user>/
ls: cannot access '/home/<user>/': No such file or directory
```

The existing file is NOT deleted by this failure (confirmed via deliberate reproduction — `cat` immediately after shows the file intact). The write silently fails and the agent may report success or confusion if it doesn't check the error.

## Workaround

The same host directory is also mounted at `/output/` (rw) inside the container. `write_file` and `patch` do NOT resolve `/output/` to a host path — they pass it through as-is, so writes succeed:

```
write_file(path="/output/test.txt", content="world")
→ {"bytes_written":5,"resolved_path":"/output/test.txt"}  ✓
```

Same inode confirmed — `/output/test.txt` and `/opt/data/cache/documents/test.txt` are the same physical file:
```
$ stat -c '%i' /output/test.txt /opt/data/cache/documents/test.txt
3325741
3325741
```

Alternatively, `terminal` with heredoc works on the `/opt/data/` path directly:
```bash
cat > /opt/data/cache/documents/test.txt << 'EOF'
world
EOF
```

## Mount Structure (from /proc/1/mountinfo)

```
/home/<user>/.hermes/cache/documents → /output                         (rw)
/home/<user>/.hermes/cache/documents → /opt/data/cache/documents       (rw)
/home/<user>/.hermes/cache/documents → /root/.hermes/cache/documents    (ro)
```

All three are the same host LVM volume mounted at different container paths. The `write_file`/`patch` tools resolve `/opt/data/cache/documents/` to the host path, but do not resolve `/output/`.

## Impact

This has caused recurring silent write failures across multiple sessions for files like `tasks.md` — the agent attempts to update the file via `write_file`, the write fails, and the next session finds the file stale or unchanged. The bug is general to any file under `/opt/data/cache/documents/`, not specific to `tasks.md`.

## Environment

- Hermes Agent: latest (installed on host, not in Docker image)
- Terminal backend: docker
- Container image: nikolaik/python-nodejs:python3.11-nodejs20
- Host OS: Ubuntu Server
- Container HOME: /home/pn (uid 1000 maps to host uid 1000)

## Proposed Fix

**Option 1 (simplest):** In the `write_file`/`patch` path resolution logic, detect paths under `/opt/data/cache/documents/` and rewrite them to `/output/` before execution. Both are the same physical directory, but only `/output/` is not remapped by the tool.

**Option 2 (correct):** Do not resolve container paths back to host paths at all. Pass the path as-is to the `docker exec` command. The container's filesystem is the correct execution context — the tool should not second-guess the path the agent provides.

**Option 3:** Add a config option (e.g., `terminal.docker_path_map`) that lets users declare path equivalences the tool should apply before execution:
```yaml
terminal:
  docker_path_map:
    "/opt/data/cache/documents/": "/output/"
```

## Related Issues

- #32049 — Docker terminal backend path resolution (sandbox-mirror state writes)
- #45792 — Hermes inside Docker doesn't understand its own config path
- #49535 — Support multiple HERMES_WRITE_SAFE_ROOT directories

items.title: Windows: desktop Update button can never succeed on gateway-enabled installs (venv-blocker preflight aborts on the always-running gateway)

labels.name: comp/cli
labels.description: CLI entry point, hermes_cli/, setup wizard

labels.name: P1
labels.description: High — major feature broken, no workaround

labels.name: sweeper:risk-compatibility
labels.description: Sweeper risk: may break existing users, config, migrations, defaults, or upgrades

labels.name: sweeper:risk-platform-windows
labels.description: Sweeper risk: may break or behave differently on native Windows

items.body:
## Summary

Since the updater redesign (commits `95d303138`, 2026-07-28 and `30c783589`, 2026-07-29), a **default Windows install with the gateway service enabled can never complete an update from the desktop app**. Every click on Update: kills the app's own backend → runs the venv-blocker preflight → finds the always-running gateway → aborts with "Update didn't finish" → the app is left on the "Hermes couldn't start" recovery screen. The Update button is effectively unusable, and each attempt looks like a crash to the user.

The ironic part: the CLI updater already contains pause/resume logic for exactly this (`_pause_windows_gateways_for_update` / `_resume_windows_gateways_after_update`, and it prints "✓ Starting Windows gateway after update" on success) — but the desktop preflight aborts before that logic ever gets a chance to run, and the pause's gateway discovery misses some gateway spawn paths anyway (details below).

## Environment

- Hermes Agent v0.19.0, HEAD `30c783589`, install method: git
- Windows 11 Pro 10.0.26200
- Gateway installed as the setup-created autostart entries (Scheduled Task `Hermes_Gateway` + Startup-folder `Hermes_Gateway.vbs`) — i.e. the gateway is essentially always running, by design.

## Reproduction

1. Windows install with the gateway service installed (the default after gateway setup).
2. Open Hermes desktop, click **Update** (menu or banner).
3. Dialog: *"Update aborted: another Hermes process is using this installation. These processes must be stopped before updating: PID … python.exe … -m hermes_cli.main gateway run"*.
4. Because `applyUpdates` already killed its own backend before the scan, the app then shows **"Hermes couldn't start — The background gateway didn't come up"** (SIGTERM recovery screen).
5. Retry → same loop, forever. The gateway respawns via the scheduled task / login item even if the user stops it manually, so non-technical users are permanently stuck.

`desktop.log` excerpt:

```
[updates] restart: Updating Hermes — this window will close and the updater will open.
[updates] state.db pre-flight: … headerOk=true …
[updates] venv shim unlocked; safe to proceed
[updates] venv-blocked: 1 process(es) hold the install
[updates] error: Update aborted: another Hermes process is using this installation.
  PID 27664  python.exe  …\venv\Scripts\python.exe -m hermes_cli.main gateway run
[boot] Hermes backend exited before it became ready (SIGTERM).
```

## Two distinct defects

### 1. Desktop preflight treats the gateway as a fatal blocker (apps/desktop/electron/main.ts)

`applyUpdates` → `releaseBackendLockForUpdate` (line ~2719) stops only the app's **own** backends, then the Windows preflight `scanVenvBlockers(updateRoot)` (line ~2936) aborts on *any* remaining venv process — including the gateway, which the app itself (or its autostart entries) started and which `hermes update` knows how to pause and resume. The scan result even identifies the process as the gateway in the message, yet nothing attempts to stop it.

Suggested fix: before aborting, pause gateway processes the same way `hermes_cli/update_cmd.py::_pause_windows_gateways_for_update` does (or simply exclude gateway PIDs from the fatal set and let the spawned CLI updater handle them — it already pauses gateways as its first post-backup step and resumes them via `atexit`). The updater already cold-starts the gateway after a successful update (`_cold_start_windows_gateway_after_update`, update_cmd.py ~2814), so stopping it before is symmetric with existing behavior.

### 2. CLI gateway pause misses some gateway spawn paths (hermes_cli/update_cmd.py)

Even `hermes update` from a terminal can abort on the gateway *after* the pause step ran. Observed output (same session):

```
✗ Other Hermes processes are running from this install's venv:
  PID 6404  python.exe  …\venv\Scripts\python.exe -m hermes_cli.main gateway run  ← gateway
```

Note the updater's own annotation: `← gateway`. Flow (update_cmd.py ~3105–3129): `_pause_windows_gateways_for_update()` runs first, then `_detect_venv_python_processes()` still finds a live `gateway run` process and exits 2. So the pause's discovery (`find_gateway_pids`) did not see a gateway that the venv-holder scan then correctly identified as one. In our case the missed gateways were ones spawned as `gateway run --replace` (desktop-initiated) and shim-wrapped children (`hermes.exe` parent → `python.exe` child); presumably these don't land in whatever pid registry `find_gateway_pids` consults. Since `_format_venv_python_holders_message` can already classify a holder as a gateway, that same classification could feed the pause/terminate path instead of the abort path.

## Workaround we're using

```powershell
hermes gateway stop
hermes update -y     # updater cold-starts the gateway again when done
```

This completes reliably. But it requires knowing the incantation — the GUI Update button, which is what most users will press, cannot succeed on a gateway-enabled Windows install.

## Impact

- Every gateway-enabled Windows install: GUI updates permanently broken since 2026-07-28.
- Each failed attempt SIGTERMs the running backend, so the failure presents as a crash ("Hermes couldn't start"), which invites users toward "Repair install" or full reinstalls that don't fix anything.

items.title: [Bug]: credential-pool write-through to global root self-disables after the first refresh per profile (regression of #48415 / #43589)

labels.name: comp/agent
labels.description: Core agent runtime: loop, agent_init, prompt builder, context-compression, responses endpoint

labels.name: P1
labels.description: High — major feature broken, no workaround

labels.name: sweeper:risk-security-boundary
labels.description: Sweeper risk: may affect sandboxing, auth, credentials, or sensitive data

items.body:
### Summary

The global-root write-through added for #48415 / #43589 protects a profile's **first** pool refresh only. The same code path then persists `providers.<id>` into the profile store, which permanently flips the write-through decision to `False` for every subsequent refresh in that profile.

Net effect on a multi-profile install: root keeps a revoked single-use refresh token forever, and the cross-profile rotation hazard those issues closed comes back — silently, after one refresh per profile.

### Version

`v0.19.0` (`2026.7.20`), Docker install, 9 profiles sharing one ChatGPT account via `openai-codex`.

### Root cause

`agent/credential_pool.py::_sync_device_code_entry_to_auth_store`:

```python
auth_store = _load_auth_store()                    # profile store
# Decide BEFORE writing whether this profile is reading the grant from
# the global root (no own providers.<id> block) vs. genuinely shadowing it.
write_through_to_root = bool(_wt_provider_id) and not (
    isinstance(auth_store.get("providers"), dict)
    and isinstance(auth_store["providers"].get(_wt_provider_id), dict)
)
...
elif self.provider == "openai-codex":
    state = _load_provider_state(auth_store, "openai-codex")   # (a) root fallback
    if not isinstance(state, dict):
        return
    tokens = state.get("tokens")
    if not isinstance(tokens, dict):
        return
    tokens["access_token"] = entry.access_token
    ...
    _store_provider_state(auth_store, "openai-codex", state, set_active=False)  # (b)

_save_auth_store(auth_store)                       # (c) persists to the PROFILE
if write_through_to_root and _wt_provider_id:
    _write_through_provider_state_to_global_root(_wt_provider_id, state)
```

The `Decide BEFORE writing` comment correctly handles ordering **within** one call. The problem is **across** calls:

1. **First refresh** — the profile has no `providers.openai-codex`, so `write_through_to_root = True`. At (a), `_load_provider_state` falls back to the root state (documented behaviour). At (b), `_store_provider_state` does `providers[provider_id] = state` **on the profile's store**, and (c) persists it. The write-through fires. Correct — once.
2. **Every later refresh** — the profile now owns a `providers.openai-codex` block (created at step 1, not by the user), so the condition evaluates to `False`. Root is never updated again.

The predicate is computed from a key that the same function creates three lines later, so it is self-sealing. `hermes_cli/auth.py::_store_provider_state` is unconditional:

```python
providers = auth_store.setdefault("providers", {})
...
providers[provider_id] = state
```

This is not user misconfiguration: nothing in our tooling writes `providers.openai-codex`, and profiles are created without it.

### Evidence

Real install, 9 profiles, one ChatGPT account, after several weeks of normal operation:

| store | `providers.openai-codex` | tokens in it | `credential_pool.openai-codex` |
|---|---|---|---|
| root `~/.hermes/auth.json` | present | **empty `{}`** | 1 entry, valid |
| 7 of 8 profiles | present | **empty `{}`** | 1 entry, valid |
| 1 newer profile (never refreshed its codex pool yet) | **absent** | — | 1 entry, valid |

The one profile still missing the block is the only one that has never completed a codex pool refresh — exactly what the mechanism above predicts.

Two distinct refresh tokens are live at once (masked): the 9 auth stores agree on `<tokenA>` (access valid), while the older shared copy still holds `<tokenB>` (access expired 9 days earlier). Any consumer resolving from a stale store gets `refresh_token_reused` / `invalid_grant`.

Note the blocks are persisted with an **empty** `tokens: {}` — the codex branch writes into `state["tokens"]` obtained from the root fallback, which was itself an empty dict, so the stored block carries no credential. It only serves to disable the write-through and to short-circuit `_sync_codex_entry_from_auth_store`, whose guard is `if store_access and (...)`.

### Steps to reproduce

1. `hermes auth add openai-codex` at global scope. Create two profiles, neither with its own codex auth.
2. Run a turn in profile A until its pool entry refreshes. Observe `providers.openai-codex` appear in `~/.hermes/profiles/A/auth.json` and the rotated chain land in root.
3. Run another turn in profile A that triggers a second refresh.
4. Inspect root: `providers.openai-codex.tokens` still holds the token from step 2, not the rotated one.
5. Run a turn in profile B. Once its access token expires, its refresh fails with `refresh_token_reused` / `invalid_grant`.

### Expected

The write-through should follow the store the state was actually **resolved from**, not the presence of a key that this function itself creates.

### Suggested fix

The codebase already exposes the right signal — `hermes_cli/auth.py::_load_provider_state_with_source` returns `(state, source_path)` precisely so that "refresh paths that rotate single-use OAuth refresh tokens … write the updated token chain back to the same store they read". It is used inside `auth.py` but not on the credential-pool path.

Deciding on `source_path == _global_auth_file_path()` instead of key presence would make the behaviour idempotent across refreshes and cover the `nous` / `xai-oauth` branches identically.

A second, smaller point: the codex/xai branches `return` early when `state` or `state["tokens"]` is not a dict, so a profile that legitimately has no provider block and no root fallback silently skips the sync. Worth confirming that is intended.

### Impact

Multi-profile installs sharing one OAuth account. The workaround is an external cron that re-propagates the freshest credential across every `auth.json` and restarts the gateways on rotation — which is what #48415 set out to remove.

Happy to test a patch against this install.

items.title: tests/hermes_cli/ exits 0 after running 3,494 of 10,437 tests — run_gateway() test reaches os._exit(0) and kills pytest

labels.name: duplicate
labels.description: This issue or pull request already exists

labels.name: comp/cli
labels.description: CLI entry point, hermes_cli/, setup wizard

labels.name: sweeper:cannot-reproduce
labels.description: Sweeper: could not reproduce on current main

labels.name: sweeper:risk-message-delivery
labels.description: Sweeper risk: may drop, duplicate, misroute, or suppress messages

items.body:
## Summary

`pytest tests/hermes_cli/` **exits 0 after running only 3,494 of 10,437 collected tests**. There is no summary line and no failure — it looks like a clean pass. 6,943 tests silently never execute.

The cause is `test_run_gateway_refreshes_outdated_unit_on_boot`, which drives `run_gateway()` to completion. That function terminates via `os._exit(0)`, which kills the pytest process itself — bypassing pytest's reporting entirely and returning the child's exit code 0.

Reproduced on current `main` (`c3ffe2738`) with a clean venv, Python 3.13.2, pytest 9.0.2.

## Reproduction

```bash
python -m pytest tests/hermes_cli/ -q
# ... progress stops at [ 33%]
# no summary line, no "N passed", exit code 0
echo $?   # 0
```

Single test in isolation — note it produces neither PASSED nor FAILED:

```bash
python -m pytest "tests/hermes_cli/test_gateway_service.py::TestSystemdServiceRefresh::test_run_gateway_refreshes_outdated_unit_on_boot" -v
# collected 1 item
# tests/hermes_cli/test_gateway_service.py::...::test_run_gateway_refreshes_outdated_unit_on_boot
# <process exits here — no verdict, no summary>
```

Counts:

| | |
|---|---|
| collected | 10,437 |
| actually run | 3,494 |
| never executed | **6,943** |
| reported exit code | **0** |

## Mechanism

`tests/hermes_cli/test_gateway_service.py:217` patches `gateway.run.start_gateway` and then calls `gateway_cli.run_gateway()` directly (`:242`). It does not patch the exit path, so:

1. `run_gateway()` — `hermes_cli/gateway.py:4819`
2. → `_hard_exit_after_gateway_teardown(0)` — `hermes_cli/gateway.py:5037` (also `:5066`)
3. → `gateway.run._exit_after_graceful_shutdown(0)` — `gateway/run.py:25337`
4. → `os._exit(0)`

The production choice is correct and intentional — `_exit_after_graceful_shutdown`'s docstring explains `os._exit` is used over `sys.exit` precisely to avoid the `Py_FinalizeEx` → `wait_for_thread_shutdown` hang in #53107. The problem is only that a test reaches it.

The code already anticipates this. `hermes_cli/gateway.py:5038` reads:

```python
        _hard_exit_after_gateway_teardown(0)
        return  # unreachable in production (os._exit); guard for test stubs
```

but that `return` guards nothing, because step 2 above is the real function rather than a stub — nothing in this test replaces it.

## Secondary effect: the test cannot fail

Because `os._exit(0)` fires at `:242`, the test's own assertions at `:244-245` are unreachable:

```python
        gateway_cli.run_gateway()                                  # <- process dies here

        assert unit_path.read_text(encoding="utf-8") == "new unit\n"   # never runs
        assert ["systemctl", "--user", "daemon-reload"] in calls        # never runs
```

So it is simultaneously breaking the suite and not testing anything.

## Why this matters beyond the one test

Any CI step shaped like `pytest tests/hermes_cli/ && echo ok` passes unconditionally. The failure mode is not a red build — it is a **green** build covering a third of the suite. For what it's worth, the truncation is not silent in content: 14 genuine failures are visible in the progress dots before the process dies, in `test_config.py`, `test_console_engine.py`, `test_dashboard_auth_password_login.py`, `test_env_custom_keys.py`, `test_env_export_line_lifecycle.py`, and `test_gateway_runtime_health.py`. Those are separate from this issue, but they are currently unreportable because the run never reaches a summary.

## Suggested fix

Patch the exit boundary in the test, so the assertions become reachable:

```python
        monkeypatch.setattr(
            gateway_cli, "_hard_exit_after_gateway_teardown", lambda code: None
        )
```

`_hard_exit_after_gateway_teardown` is a closure defined inside `run_gateway` (`:5014`), so it may be cleaner to lift it to module scope, or to have the test patch `gateway.run._exit_after_graceful_shutdown` instead — whichever you prefer as the supported seam.

Worth considering more broadly: a session-scoped autouse fixture that replaces `os._exit` with something raising a sentinel exception would turn "test kills the runner" into an ordinary test failure for the whole suite, rather than relying on each future test that touches a hard-exit path to remember.

I'm happy to send a PR for whichever shape you'd prefer.

items.title: `distribution_owned` does not constrain profile distribution copy/update payload

labels.name: comp/cli
labels.description: CLI entry point, hermes_cli/, setup wizard

labels.name: P1
labels.description: High — major feature broken, no workaround

labels.name: sweeper:risk-compatibility
labels.description: Sweeper risk: may break existing users, config, migrations, defaults, or upgrades

items.body:
## Environment

- Hermes tag: `v2026.7.20` (annotated tag object `c7d08de287556b3d339df336b180a39d4980ebd7`, dereferenced commit `3ef6bbd201263d354fd83ec55b3c306ded2eb72a`)
- Also verified present in the released **v0.19.0** source: `_copy_dist_payload()` at `hermes_cli/profile_distribution.py:545-587` still iterates every staged entry with only `USER_OWNED_EXCLUDE` filtering, retains the wholesale directory replacement at `:573-585`, and `owned_paths()` (`:238-242`) is not consulted from the mutation path (call sites `:634`, `:692` pass the manifest but the copy loop ignores the allowlist).
- macOS; reproduced entirely in a disposable `HERMES_HOME`

## Summary

`DistributionManifest.from_dict()` parses `distribution_owned`, and `owned_paths()` returns either that explicit list or `DEFAULT_DIST_OWNED`. The install/update mutation path does not consult `owned_paths()`. `_copy_dist_payload()` iterates every top-level staged entry and copies each entry unless its name is in `USER_OWNED_EXCLUDE` or it receives one of the special `.env.template` / `config.yaml` cases.

As a result, an explicit manifest such as:

```yaml
name: repro
distribution_owned:
  - SOUL.md
```

still installs unrelated top-level entries such as `unlisted.txt`, `.github/`, `docs/`, `ops/`, tests and plugins. On update, a staged directory also replaces the complete destination directory, deleting target-only children.

## Relevant source (at `v2026.7.20`)

- Parse and persistence: `hermes_cli/profile_distribution.py:198-242`
- Copy loop: `hermes_cli/profile_distribution.py:545-587`
- Whole-directory replacement: `hermes_cli/profile_distribution.py:572-585`
- Fresh install call: `hermes_cli/profile_distribution.py:632-639`

No call from the install/update mutation path to `DistributionManifest.owned_paths()` was found at either tag.

## Minimal reproduction

1. Create a local distribution source containing:

```text
distribution.yaml
SOUL.md
unlisted.txt
skills/managed/SKILL.md
```

2. Set `distribution.yaml` to:

```yaml
name: repro
version: 1.0.0
distribution_owned:
  - SOUL.md
```

3. Install it into a disposable profile using the released `install_distribution()` path.
4. Observe that `unlisted.txt` and `skills/` are installed despite not being listed.
5. Add `skills/local-only/SKILL.md` only in the target profile.
6. Update from the same source.
7. Observe that `skills/local-only/` is removed when the staged `skills/` directory replaces the destination directory.

A saved reproduction against a disposable root recorded:

```text
listed source entry installed: true
unlisted source entry not installed: false
target-only child survives update: false
```

Full reproduction matrix available on request.

## Expected behaviour

The copy/update mutation path should honour the manifest's resolved owned paths. Entries absent from the allowlist should not be installed or updated. Directory update semantics should be documented explicitly; if target-only children are intentionally removed, the manifest should make that ownership boundary unambiguous before mutation.

## Actual behaviour

The allowlist is declaration-only. Every non-hard-excluded top-level staged entry is copied, and staged directories replace corresponding destination directories wholesale.

## Why this matters

- A distribution can ship more source than its manifest declares.
- Repository-only directories and bespoke credential filenames are not prevented from entering the installed profile unless covered by separate repository policy.
- Target-only children under an included directory can be removed during update.
- Users may reasonably treat the documented ownership list as the update boundary even though the released mutation path does not enforce it.

## Suggested direction

Resolve `manifest.owned_paths()` before copying, validate each entry, and iterate only the resolved allowlist. Define directory ownership/update semantics explicitly and add regression tests for:

1. listed entry installed;
2. unlisted entry excluded;
3. top-level hard exclusions preserved regardless of the manifest;
4. target-only children handled according to the documented ownership model;
5. `config.yaml` preservation and `--force-config` behaviour retained.

items.title: [Bug]: Desktop — Esc does not interrupt a running turn (Stop button works)

labels.name: sweeper:implemented-on-main
labels.description: Sweeper: behavior already present on current main

items.body:
## Bug Description

On the desktop app, pressing **Esc** during an active assistant turn does not interrupt generation. The Stop button (square icon next to the composer) works correctly, but the Esc keybinding never fires — regardless of where focus is (composer input, message thread, or elsewhere in the chat surface).

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Open a chat session in the Hermes desktop app (macOS, packaged Electron build).
2. Send any prompt that produces a long streaming response.
3. While the response is streaming, press **Esc** — try with focus in:
   a. The composer text input
   b. The message thread (click on an assistant message first)
   c. Anywhere else in the chat surface
4. Observe: generation continues uninterrupted in all three cases.
5. Click the **Stop** button — generation halts immediately (expected behavior).

## Expected Behavior

Esc interrupts the running turn, matching Stop-button behavior, per the wiring in `apps/desktop/src/app/chat/composer/index.tsx` (line ~788–805) and `use-composer-esc-cancel.ts`.

## Actual Behavior

Esc has no effect. Generation continues until complete or until Stop is clicked.

## Suspected Cause

The global Esc handler in `use-composer-esc-cancel.ts` (line 40) bails when `getActiveComposer() !== target`. If the active-composer tracker loses sync with the mounted composer (e.g., after tab switches, tile mounts, or focus changes), the handler silently no-ops. The composer-local Esc handler (line 788–805 of `composer/index.tsx`) only fires when the composer input itself has keyboard focus — which explains why clicking into the thread and pressing Esc also fails.

The `haltRun` path itself is fine (Stop works), so this is purely a keybinding/focus-routing issue.

## Environment

- **OS:** macOS 26.5.2 (Apple Silicon, M1)
- **Hermes version:** v0.19.0 (2026.7.20), git install, upstream `41a07f5b`
- **Desktop app:** packaged Electron build at `apps/desktop/release/mac-arm64/Hermes.app`, built 2026-07-29 08:20 local
- **Config:** `busy_input_mode: interrupt` (default), no custom keybindings

## Additional Context

- The `useComposerEscCancel` hook has been in the composer since `e009ba57a` (2026-06-30).
- The running Electron process was started after the build, so the packaged code should include the hook.
- Voice-conversation barge-in (`voice-barge-in.ts`) works correctly — VAD detects speech and cuts TTS playback. This bug is specific to the keyboard interrupt path.

items.body:
### Bug Description

 Version: v2026.7.20-2761-ge0233f8fc (commit f8758dcaf)

 Description:

 The gateway repeatedly exits uncleanly (SIGKILL) when processing agent conversations. Traceback:

 File "agent/conversation_loop.py:1489", in run_conversation
     agent._copy_reasoning_content_for_api(msg, api_msg)
 File "run_agent.py:6717", in _copy_reasoning_content_for_api
     from agent.agent_runtime_helpers import copy_reasoning_content_for_api
 File "agent/agent_runtime_helpers.py:3340", in copy_reasoning_content_for_api
     from agent.message_sanitization import apply_reasoning_content_policy
 ImportError: cannot import name 'apply_reasoning_content_policy'

 The function exists at agent/message_sanitization.py:699 but the lazy import inside the function body fails at runtime
 — the agent package namespace hasn't finished loading message_sanitization when the import executes.



### Steps to Reproduce

Traceback:

 File "agent/conversation_loop.py:1489", in run_conversation
     agent._copy_reasoning_content_for_api(msg, api_msg)
 File "run_agent.py:6717", in _copy_reasoning_content_for_api
     from agent.agent_runtime_helpers import copy_reasoning_content_for_api
 File "agent/agent_runtime_helpers.py:3340", in copy_reasoning_content_for_api
     from agent.message_sanitization import apply_reasoning_content_policy
 ImportError: cannot import name 'apply_reasoning_content_policy'

 The function exists at agent/message_sanitization.py:699 and is listed in all at line 486, but the lazy import inside
 the function body fails at runtime. The agent package namespace hasn't finished loading message_sanitization when the
 import executes.

### Expected Behavior

 Gateway starts, connects all platforms, and handles agent conversations without crashing.

 Actual behavior: Gateway connects all platforms successfully, but when an agent conversation executes
 _copy_reasoning_content_for_api, the apply_reasoning_content_policy import fails with ImportError. This propagates up as an
 unhandled exception and the gateway process exits with SIGKILL (unclean exit), requiring a manual restart.

 Steps to reproduce:
 1. Start gateway (hermes gateway)
 2. Send a message to the gateway (e.g., via Telegram)
 3. Gateway connects and receives the message

items.title: Windows update blocked on gateway-enabled installs: three-layer chain (Electron → Rust bootstrapper → Python CLI) fails to coordinate gateway pause/resume

labels.name: comp/cli
labels.description: CLI entry point, hermes_cli/, setup wizard

labels.name: P1
labels.description: High — major feature broken, no workaround

labels.name: sweeper:risk-compatibility
labels.description: Sweeper risk: may break existing users, config, migrations, defaults, or upgrades

labels.name: sweeper:risk-platform-windows
labels.description: Sweeper risk: may break or behave differently on native Windows

items.body:
## Summary

On Windows gateway-enabled installs, the desktop Update button triggers a
three-layer chain (Electron → Rust bootstrapper → Python CLI) where **each
layer has a different gap** in gateway process coordination. Together they
guarantee that the desktop updater can never complete on a gateway-enabled
install without manual `hermes gateway stop` intervention.

I hit this today (HEAD `015718066`, 2026-07-29). Every click on Update killed
my backend, found the gateway still running, showed the "Update didn't finish"
dialog, then left the app on the "Hermes couldn't start" recovery screen.

Related:
- Tracking the same scenario from a user perspective: **#74326**
- `force_kill_other_hermes` misses `pythonw.exe`: **#70026**
- Desktop updater `--venv-blocked` race with gateway respawn: **#73822**

---

## Layer 1: Electron (apps/desktop/electron/main.ts)

### Path: `applyUpdates` → `releaseBackendLockForUpdate` → `scanVenvBlockers`

`releaseBackendLockForUpdate` (line 2694) only collects PIDs the desktop owns
— its primary window backend + pool backends (`backendConnectionState`,
`backendPool`). It sends them SIGTERM, then force-tree-kills them, then polls
the venv shim for 15s until it's writable.

Once the shim unlocks, `scanVenvBlockers` (line 2911, via
`venv-blocker-scan.ts`) runs a Python subprocess that calls
`_detect_venv_python_processes()` in `hermes_cli/main.py`. This scans *every*
live process whose executable or cmdline references the venv — including the
**gateway**, which was never part of the desktop's PID set and was never
stopped.

```typescript
// main.ts:2910-2920
if (IS_WINDOWS) {
  const scanOutcome = await scanVenvBlockers(updateRoot)
  if (scanOutcome.kind === 'blocked') {
    // Aborts — but the blocker is always the gateway on gateway-enabled installs
    return { ok: false, error: 'venv-blocked', message }
  }
}
```

The ironic part: the Electron code itself then spawns the CLI updater
detached via `spawnUpdaterProcess` (line 2936), and that CLI updater
(`hermes update`) starts with `_pause_windows_gateways_for_update()` as its
second step — it knows how to pause and resume gateways. But we never reach
that because the Electron preflight aborted first.

### Fix

Before the venv-blocker preflight scan, the Electron code should pause
gateway processes using the same mechanism the CLI uses. Either:

**(A)** Run a Python subprocess that calls
`_pause_windows_gateways_for_update()` (already an importable function in
`hermes_cli.main`) before `scanVenvBlockers`, then pass the resume token to
the spawned CLI updater so it doesn't double-resume.

**(B)** Or, less invasively: before aborting on `venv-blocked`, check whether
the blocking processes are gateways (the Python scan already classifies them
— `_format_venv_python_holders_message` annotates `← gateway`) and if so,
kill them with the gateway-aware path before retrying the scan:

```typescript
// Pseudo: if all blockers are gateways, pause them and rescan
if (blockersAreAllGateways(scanOutcome)) {
  await pauseWindowsGateways() // calls _pause_windows_gateways_for_update
  const rescan = await scanVenvBlockers(updateRoot)
  if (rescan.kind === 'clear') {
    // proceed with spawn
  }
}
```

---

## Layer 2: Rust Bootstrapper (apps/bootstrap-installer/src-tauri/src/update.rs)

### Path: `install-lock wait` → `force_kill_other_hermes`

`force_kill_other_hermes` (line 587) is the bootstrapper's last-resort PID
cleaner before it touches the venv. It runs `taskkill /F /T /IM hermes.exe`.

The problem: the gateway process runs as `python.exe` or `pythonw.exe`, not
`hermes.exe`. On Windows, the gateway is spawned as:

```
venv\Scripts\pythonw.exe -m hermes_cli.main gateway run
```

`taskkill /IM hermes.exe` does not touch it. The venv's `.pyd` files remain
locked, and the subsequent `Remove-Item -Recurse -Force venv` or dependency
sync fails with "Access denied."

This is well-documented in the install.ps1 installer (lines 1864–1870):
```powershell
# taskkill /IM hermes.exe is NOT enough: the gateway/agent that a
# scheduled task or watchdog autostart runs as
# `pythonw.exe -m hermes_cli.main gateway run` straight out of
# venv\Scripts\, so its image name is python/pythonw...
```

### Fix

Add `python.exe` and `pythonw.exe` to the taskkill image list, but ONLY for
processes whose command line or working directory matches the install root
(otherwise we'd kill unrelated Python processes). Or better, use the same
`detect_venv_python_processes` logic from `hermes_cli/main.py` (run it as a
subprocess) to get targeted PIDs, then `taskkill /PID` each one.

```rust
fn force_kill_other_hermes() {
    if !cfg!(target_os = "windows") { return; }
    #[cfg(target_os = "windows")]
    {
        let my_pid = std::process::id();
        // Kill hermes.exe (existing behavior)
        let _ = std::process::Command::new("taskkill")
            .args(["/F", "/T", "/IM", "hermes.exe", "/FI", &format!("PID ne {my_pid}")])
            .stdout(std::process::Stdio::null())
            .stderr(std::process::Stdio::null())
            .status();

        // Also kill python(w).exe processes running from this venv
        // (gateway/backend).  Filter by command line or working directory
        // to avoid nuking unrelated Python processes.
        let install_root = /* resolve from context */;
        let _ = std::process::Command::new("powershell")
            .args([
                "-NoProfile", "-Command",
                &format!(
                    "Get-CimInstance Win32_Process | Where-Object {{ \
                        $_.Name -match '^python(w?)\.exe$' -and \
                        $_.CommandLine -like '*{}venv*' \
                    }} | ForEach-Object {{ taskkill /F /PID $_.ProcessId }}",
                    install_root.to_string_lossy()
                ),
            ])
            .stdout(std::process::Stdio::null())
            .stderr(std::process::Stdio::null())
            .status();
    }
}
```

---

## Layer 3: Python CLI (hermes_cli/main.py)

### Path: `_pause_windows_gateways_for_update` → `_detect_venv_python_processes`

The CLI updater flow (line 12228–12252):
1. `_pause_windows_gateways_for_update()` runs — discovers gateways via
   `find_gateway_pids()` + `find_profile_gateway_processes()`, force-kills
   them, and returns a resume token.
2. `_detect_venv_python_processes()` runs — scans all processes from the venv.
3. If it finds any, **it aborts and calls `_resume_windows_gateways_after_update`
   in the same breath**.

The gap: step 2 can find a process that step 1 missed. This can happen with
gateways spawned as `gateway run --replace` (desktop-initiated) or through
shim-wrapped children (`hermes.exe` parent → `python.exe` child) that don't
register in whatever PID registry `find_gateway_pids()` consults.

When step 2 finds such a process, it:
- Prints `← gateway` annotation (proving it CAN identify it as a gateway)
- But still classifies it as a fatal blocker and exits 2
- Calls `_resume_windows_gateways_after_update` (which then respawns even
  more gateways, making the problem worse on retry)

The code at line 12247–12252:
```python
if _is_windows() and not getattr(args, "force_venv", False):
    _venv_holders = _detect_venv_python_processes()
    if _venv_holders:
        print(_format_venv_python_holders_message(_venv_holders))
        _resume_windows_gateways_after_update(_windows_gateway_resume)  # re-spawns!
        sys.exit(2)
```

### Fix

If `_detect_venv_python_processes()` finds a process, re-check whether it's
a gateway before aborting. The information is already in the scan (the
function returns `(pid, name, cmdline)` triples, and
`_format_venv_python_holders_message` already classifies them). Instead of
unconditionally aborting, when all remaining blockers are gateway processes:

1. Run the gateway pause again with expanded discovery (include the PIDs
   found by the venv process scan as an additional input to the kill set)
2. Re-scan
3. Only abort if non-gateway processes remain

```python
if _is_windows() and not getattr(args, "force_venv", False):
    _venv_holders = _detect_venv_python_processes()
    if _venv_holders:
        # Check if all remaining blockers are gateways
        gateway_only = all(
            "gateway" in cmdline.lower() for _, _, cmdline in _venv_holders
        )
        if gateway_only:
            # These gateways slipped past _pause_windows_gateways_for_update.
            # Re-pause with expanded PID set instead of aborting.
            extra_pids = [pid for pid, _, _ in _venv_holders]
            _retry_pause_gateways(extra_pids)
            _venv_holders = _detect_venv_python_processes()
        if _venv_holders:
            print(_format_venv_python_holders_message(_venv_holders))
            _resume_windows_gateways_after_update(_windows_gateway_resume)
            sys.exit(2)
```

---

## Environment

- Hermes Agent HEAD `015718066` (2026-07-29), git install
- Windows 11 Pro 10.0.26200
- Gateway installed as Scheduled Task (`Hermes_Gateway`)

## Workaround (for anyone hitting this now)

```powershell
hermes gateway stop
hermes update --yes
```

The CLI updater correctly pauses/resumes gateways when the desktop preflight
is not in the way. `hermes gateway start` or a reboot will re-enable the
gateway after the update.

## Summary

The optional DingTalk lazy dependency is pinned to `alibabacloud-dingtalk==2.2.42` in `tools/lazy_deps.py`. Its resolved `alibabacloud-tea-openapi==0.4.4` metadata requires `cryptography<47` on supported modern Python versions, while the current Hermes dependency set installs a newer `cryptography` release.

`pip check` therefore reports an incompatible environment. The SDK imports successfully, but the declared conflict means DingTalk users can encounter untested behaviour in cryptographic SDK paths.

## Reproduction

1. Install Hermes with the optional/lazy DingTalk dependencies available.
2. Run:

```bash
python -m pip check
```

Current result includes:

```text
alibabacloud-tea-openapi 0.4.4 has requirement cryptography<47.0.0,>=3.0.0, but a newer cryptography version is installed
```

## Suggested resolution

Refresh the DingTalk lazy dependency pin and its transitive Tea OpenAPI dependency, then validate the DingTalk adapter. The currently available `alibabacloud-tea-openapi==0.4.5` expands its modern-Python `cryptography` upper bound to `<49`, which covers the current Hermes resolution.

## Expected outcome

- `pip check` reports no DingTalk/cryptography conflict.
- DingTalk remains optional and lazy-installed.
- The adapter import and a focused DingTalk smoke test remain healthy.

This report intentionally contains no deployment-specific configuration, credentials, or identifiers.

items.title: Desktop SSH mode: version-check runs 'python --version <script>' (wrong arg order) → always reports 'Python x.y.z' and falsely claims --ssh-session-token-file/--ssh-owner-nonce are unsupported on up-to-date git/source installs; remoteHermesPath override is also ignored for this check

labels.name: sweeper:risk-compatibility
labels.description: Sweeper risk: may break existing users, config, migrations, defaults, or upgrades

items.body:
## Summary

Desktop SSH mode ("Connect via SSH") fails on a git/source install (venv-based, not a pip/pipx console-script install) with:

```
The remote Hermes install does not support --ssh-session-token-file and --ssh-owner-nonce.
Update Hermes on the remote host to continue using Desktop SSH mode.
```

...even though the remote install is up to date (v0.19.0) and `hermes serve --help` on the remote host clearly lists both flags. Setting the `remoteHermesPath` override in the desktop app's SSH connection settings does **not** work around it — the SSH lifecycle version-check step ignores the override and keeps probing its own auto-detected path.

## Root cause (confirmed via manual reproduction over SSH)

For a git/source install, `hermes` on the remote host is not a single self-contained binary — it's a bash wrapper (`~/.local/bin/hermes`) that does:

```bash
#!/usr/bin/env bash
unset PYTHONPATH
unset PYTHONHOME
exec "/home/valentin/.hermes/hermes-agent/venv/bin/python" "/home/valentin/.hermes/hermes-agent/hermes" "$@"
```

During the SSH bootstrap's version-detection step, the desktop app logs:

```
[ssh-lifecycle] located hermes at /home/valentin/.hermes/hermes-agent/venv/bin/python
[ssh-lifecycle] remote hermes version: Python 3.11.15
```

It has correctly located the venv's `python` interpreter as part of a "venv + script" install, but when checking the version it appears to run something equivalent to:

```
<venv>/bin/python --version /home/valentin/.hermes/hermes-agent/hermes
```

i.e. `--version` is passed **to the python interpreter itself**, before the script path. Python's `--version` flag short-circuits: when given before a script argument, Python prints only its own interpreter version and exits *without ever executing the script* — this is standard CPython argv parsing behavior, not specific to Hermes. I reproduced this exactly on the remote host:

```
$ /home/valentin/.hermes/hermes-agent/venv/bin/python --version /home/valentin/.hermes/hermes-agent/hermes
Python 3.11.15
```

That `Python 3.11.15` string is exactly what shows up in the app's log as "remote hermes version". Since it can never be parsed as a real Hermes version, the app presumably concludes the remote is on some old/unknown version and bails out with the "does not support these flags" message — even though the flags genuinely exist:

```
$ /home/valentin/.hermes/hermes-agent/venv/bin/python /home/valentin/.hermes/hermes-agent/hermes --version
Hermes Agent v0.19.0 (2026.7.20) · upstream a4973c3f
Install directory: /home/valentin/.hermes/hermes-agent
Install method: git
...
Up to date

$ /home/valentin/.hermes/hermes-agent/venv/bin/python /home/valentin/.hermes/hermes-agent/hermes serve --help
usage: hermes serve [-h] [--port PORT] [--host HOST] [--insecure] [--skip-build]
                    [--isolated] [--stop] [--status]
                    [--ssh-session-token-file PATH] [--ssh-owner-nonce NONCE]
...
```

i.e. running interpreter and script in the correct order (script path before `--version`/other args) works fine and reports the real version and the two flags.

## The `remoteHermesPath` override is also ignored

The desktop app's "Connect via SSH" screen has a "Hermes path (optional)" field ("Full path to the remote hermes binary. Blank = auto-detect."). Setting it to the working wrapper path:

```
~/Library/Application Support/Hermes/connection.json:
{
  "mode": "ssh",
  "remote": {
    "mode": "ssh",
    "host": "46.224.225.69",
    "user": "valentin",
    "keyPath": "/Users/valentin/.ssh/hetznervalentin_ed25519",
    "remoteHermesPath": "/home/valentin/.local/bin/hermes"
  },
  "profiles": {}
}
```

is correctly persisted, but the SSH lifecycle version-check step still logs `located hermes at /home/valentin/.hermes/hermes-agent/venv/bin/python` (the auto-detected venv python, not the configured wrapper) and still fails with the same error. So the override appears to only be wired up for a later step (if any) and not honored during the capability/version probe.

Ran `hermes update` on both the remote host and locally (the desktop app itself is built from source via `hermes desktop`/`hermes gui`) — no change in behavior.

## Steps to reproduce

1. Install hermes-agent on a remote Linux host via the standard git/source method (`curl -fsSL https://hermes-agent.nousresearch.com/install.sh | bash`), so that `hermes` resolves to a `~/.local/bin/hermes` wrapper around a venv (not a pip console-script entry point).
2. In the macOS Hermes desktop app, go to Connection mode → **Connect via SSH**, fill in a working `Host` (IP works; hostname resolution is a separate, unrelated issue), `User`, and `Identity file` pointing at a valid key.
3. (Optional, to show the override is ignored) Also fill in **Hermes path** with the known-good wrapper path, e.g. `/home/valentin/.local/bin/hermes`.
4. Save and reconnect.

**Expected:** desktop boots the remote backend over SSH.

**Actual:** `Desktop boot failed: The remote Hermes install does not support --ssh-session-token-file and --ssh-owner-nonce. Update Hermes on the remote host to continue using Desktop SSH mode.` — regardless of the remote install already being up to date and regardless of the Hermes path override.

## Environment

- Desktop app: built locally from source (`sourceMode: false` in `desktop-build-stamp.json`, built 2026-07-29, `apps/desktop/release/mac-arm64/Hermes.app`). `Info.plist` reports `CFBundleShortVersionString` 0.17.0, which looks stale relative to the actual source tree in use (the SSH bootstrap / `--ssh-session-token-file` / `--ssh-owner-nonce` machinery clearly postdates that).
- Remote host: Ubuntu 24.04, hermes-agent installed via the official install script (git/source method), `hermes --version` → `Hermes Agent v0.19.0 (2026.7.20) · upstream a4973c3f`, `Up to date`.
- macOS: Apple Silicon (mac-arm64 build).

## Suggested fix

In the SSH lifecycle's version-detection step, invoke the script before any flags (`<python> <hermes_script_or_wrapper_path> --version`), not `<python> --version <hermes_script_or_wrapper_path>`. And/or honor `remoteHermesPath` for this step when it's set, instead of always re-deriving the python interpreter + script path via auto-detection.

items.title: Kanban SQLite index corruption (idx_events_*) under dispatcher bursts + concurrent short-lived CLI writes

labels.name: needs-decision
labels.description: Awaiting maintainer decision before any implementation

labels.name: sweeper:implemented-on-main
labels.description: Sweeper: behavior already present on current main

labels.name: sweeper:risk-session-state
labels.description: Sweeper risk: may lose/corrupt/mis-associate session or context state

items.body:
**Environment:** hermes-agent 0.18.2 → reproduced again on 0.19.0 (2026.7.20); Python 3.13.5; Debian container (Docker, bind-mounted /opt/data); kanban board with ~40 active cards, gateway dispatcher (dispatch_in_gateway: true, 60s interval) plus frequent short-lived `hermes kanban` CLI invocations from an orchestrating agent.

**Symptom:** four corruption events within ~24h. Every time, `integrity_check` reports only index inconsistencies — `wrong # of entries in index idx_events_run` / `idx_events_task` / `idx_tasks_assignee_status` — table data is intact and a plain `REINDEX` fully heals the DB (verified all 4 times). Hermes then refuses to open the DB (good fail-closed behavior) and writes a .corrupt.bak.

**Correlation:** all four events coincided with heavy write bursts: bulk card creation (~19 cards), bulk comment/block/archive sweeps (~100 ops), always while the gateway dispatcher was live and (in at least two cases) while workers were being spawned/reaped. Journal mode is WAL; quiet periods never corrupted. A 5-min integrity-probe loop we added has observed HEALTHY continuously outside burst windows.

**Not the cause (checked):** busy_timeout is set (both the connect timeout and explicit PRAGMA in _sqlite_connect); single filesystem/kernel (no NFS); the bounded cross-process init lock is present (we read the #36644 notes in kanban_db.py).

**Hypothesis:** an index-update path that isn't crash-safe when a worker process is SIGKILLed mid-write (dispatcher max-runtime reaping), or a WAL/-shm handoff race among many short-lived processes hitting first-connect concurrently.

**Workarounds in production:** periodic integrity probe with index-only auto-REINDEX; smaller write batches. Happy to provide the .corrupt.bak files or run instrumented builds.

Filed on behalf of a production deployment; corruption is 100% recoverable so far but recurring.
